speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion for time allocation on Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act and related statutes, reflects the urgent priority the Government places upon getting this important tax legislation into committee for detailed examination.
The Bill touches upon a wide variety of issues, including tax fairness, fiscal responsibility and taxpayers' rights. There has been ample debate on the principles of the Bill. 1 would remind Hon. Members of the six-day budget debate which took place in May and early June, following the budget presentation. Since the introduction of the Bill on November 29, it has been debated on another four days. In all, about 50 Members have taken part in those debates. They focused on a wide variety of experience and points of view, and their comments are of course on the record.
It is important to note that on this occasion we are breaking new ground in the parliamentary consideration of tax law. For many years it has been the practice to conduct the detailed examination of tax legislation within the House of Commons itself, sitting as the Committee of the Whole.
Our new procedure calls for a reference to a committee where, unlike in the House, experts from the private sector can appear to present comments and suggestions from taxpayers and professionals who work in the tax field. Members are no
doubt aware that, by agreement of all Parties, this particular Bill is to be sent to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, rather than to a legislative committee.
This committee procedure is a major step forward and should not be delayed. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stated on Monday, when he gave notice of this motion, many taxpayers have already expressed to him their concerns about the timely passage of the Bill to provide some certainty in tax planning. Many of the measures are of major importance to the business community, particularly to small business enterprises. These will have positive effects on the economic growth of the country, and Canadians are already responding to them in job-creating and investment opportunities.
For example, there are the provisions regarding capital gains; small business bonds, extended for another two years; and special investment tax credit, extended until the end of 1986. Small businesses may now obtain equity financing from pension and RRSP funds. Artists will be able to write off the costs of creating a work of art in the year that the expenses were actually incurred. Previously, as the House knows, they had to wait until it was sold.
1 should like to take this opportunity to point out briefly to Hon. Members that the Government's policies are already bringing about positive and encouraging results. We know that economic indicators show that Canada is well launched on the road to economic renewal. The prime bank lending rate is well down from previous levels, inflation is lower and mortgage rates have declined. Employment is up, consumer spending is up and confidence in the future is up. There is a feeling that our country is moving in a more positive direction. We are becoming more confident and productive.
The Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) complained about the length of time taken to bring the Bill before the House. I suggest to him, given the size of the Bill and the wide range of issues it covers, that there was no inordinate delay. In addition to the extensive drafting involved, which incorporated many technical points raised in the post-budget representations to the Minister, a 150-page book of technical notes was prepared to explain the numerous amendments.
On the same point, other budget Bills of recent years have taken considerable time to prepare. The Income Tax Act revisions stemming from the Budget of June, 1982, which were not nearly as extensive as the ones now before us, did not arrive for First reading until December of that year. In the case of the April 1983 Budget, the tax Bill came to the House nearly eight months later. This indicates no unreasonable delay but rather, I would suggest, a commendable initiative in bringing forward this Bill. In the case of the 1983 budget Bill,

December 5, 1985
Time Allocation
the House completed debate on second reading in four days and spent only one day in Committee of the Whole. In the case of the 1982 tax Bill, six days we spent at second reading stage and six days in committee.
As I said, on this occasion the committee examination will have a far wider scope than anything done in past years, and it is important that we get to it as quickly as possible. Therefore, I appeal to all Members to support the motion for time allocation which will move the Bill expeditiously to committee.

speechtext:
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I and my colleagues in this House are amazed that the Government would seek to terminate the discussion in this House on the principles of this legislation. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, what we have here is a major amendment to our taxation system which will change many basic principles that have been an integral part of this system for many years. The Government wants to change these principles, and for our part, we wish to debate these changes in the House. [English]
I find it incredible that the Government, having taken nine months to produce a Budget, having taken another six months to produce a tax Bill, given the obvious complexity of these fundamental issues of principle with which it was wrestling, would expect us to satisfy ourselves or the people of Canada, our constituents, that we had had a full opportunity to debate the principles of the Bill in this House for a mere 11 hours and 24 minutes. That is the amount of time devoted to this debate today. After 15 months of preparation of Budget, of drafting, we are given 11 hours and 24 minutes to debate the fundamental principles that are at stake here. It is outrageous.
Any reasonable person looking at this document with its 143 clauses going in the most detailed way into some parts of our system, which, as I said a moment ago in French, existed for many years, and being told that this document should be debated in principle in under 12 hours would find scandalous the treatment of Members on this side of the Chamber.
Let us look for just a moment at some of the issues in principle which we have only begun to debate. Believe me, we will serve the people of Canada well if we can dispose of some of these issues of principle in a positive way here on the floor of the House before moving this extraordinary document into committee.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) mentioned the lifetime capital gains exemption in Clause 58. [Translation]
We have told the Government that this proposal has been badly thought out and that it is certainly not helpful for our taxation system at this time. We even suggested other ways of dealing with capital gains, not here in the House, but elsewhere. These are major issues which should be discussed here.

If they do not accept our word for it, what about the independent experts who have looked at this provision? The Canadian Tax Foundation met in Quebec City a few weeks ago. We have comments from Ernst & Whinney saying it "will have a disastrous effect structurally on the tax system". What could be more of an issue in principle than that this provision will have a disastrous effect upon the structure of the tax system? Let me quote more from this report of that meeting. It states:
-after studying the proposal in more detail, the experts say it is badly flawed. As they wrestle with the massive legislation based on the budget proposal- which was tabled in the form of a ways and means motion last week-there is some embarrassment that they were unable to convey this message earlier.
They say it will create enormous complexity, that there will be scores of teams of tax lawyers, accountants and tax advisers seeking their way around the application of these provisions. They conclude that it will not in any way contribute to investment or job creation.
I find it interesting that the Minister of National Revenue, who has a vested interest in tax simplification, would come into the House this morning to deliver the message to us, his colleagues, that the Government wants to terminate debate. I would think the Minister of National Revenue would regard us as allies in this cause, trying to clean up this horrendous mess, make his life more simple and make the Tax Act more effective.

Not only allies but perpetrators, says the House Leader for the New Democratic Party.

Mr. Speaker, as I have already said, this proposal to change the structure of our law on capital gains is a fundamental matter of principle.

However, we have other issues as well. We have the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, something which the Government has determined it will eliminate. That plan was introduced to stimulate home ownership. It was designed to give young people the opportunity to save for their first home. That plan was introduced after much debate and much thought as a means of helping young people and of stimulating the housing sector of this country. There are major issues of principle involved in that approach.
Not only has it been eliminated, but the funds to be withdrawn from that plan are tax exempt under this proposed Bill and can be applied for any purpose whatsoever, completely and totally unrelated to the principle underlying the introduction of that provision in the first instance. I say to my colleagues on both sides of the House that surely that is an issue which deserves a full airing of the fundamental principles involved here on the floor of the House of Commons and not in committee.
December 5, 1985

Let me draw another example to the attention of the House, the reduction of the annual indexing. The tax brackets were indexed. In fact, that indexing was introduced by the now Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), our Leader, then Minister of Finance back in the early 1970s. The whole purpose of it was to put some restraint on the amount of funds that flowed automatically into the coffers of Government through an erosion of spending power and the taxation of inflationary income. There is a fundamental principle involved. In fact, not only is that principle destroyed by this provision, namely to constrain Government to limit spending, but it represents a massive tax grab-massive. The Government's own numbers shown in the document which was leaked on or about budget night by the Department of Finance show that in the year 1990-91, an additional $4.3 billion will flow to the federal Government by virtue of the elimination of that provision.
Some spokesmen for the Government have had the gall to compare this approach to that which we took when we introduced the famous and very successful six and five restraint program back in 1982. There is a major difference in principle. The six and five program preserved full indexation up to 6 per cent and up to 5 per cent. It placed pressure and it gave a real incentive to the people of Canada, employers and employees alike, to bring down their demands, to take inflationary pressure out of the system. It was successful.
By 1983 when the 6 per cent number was there for the indexation of the income tax brackets, in fact inflation was lower. The result was, of course, that no one suffered. In fact, they still had full protection against inflation.

What we have here is the complete opposite. In this case, the taxpayers are automatically penalized because there is no protection against inflation under 3 per cent. It is therefore the complete opposite. This is another question of principle, a basic principle which concerns the indexation of our taxation system.

This very issue of indexation and what role it should play in our income tax system and in our various programs is one of great principle which in itself deserves at least 12 hours of debate in this Chamber. The thought presented by the Minister of National Revenue to this House and the motion to limit debate on a Bill of this importance, a Bill with this number of fundamental changes to our income tax system, is totally unacceptable.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take a long time dealing with this Bill but I would like to put on the record some concerns I have about the process through which we are going. This is not really a time to debate the Bill itself but rather to debate whether or not it is necessary for the Government to bring in time allocation in order to put forward its legislative program.
Time Allocation
I think it is fair to say that the overwhelming majority of people in the country do not understand what is going on here. It confuses them when we claim, and I think quite fairly, that we can manage the affairs of the country but somehow cannot manage the affairs of Parliament. They see us constantly wrangling over whether or not it is necessary for the Government to proceed with its legislative program and what would be an adequate length of time for the Opposition to express adequately its concerns about what is contained in various pieces of legislation.
The other day as I was going through an airport, I met a woman who, after having watched parliamentary television, recognized me. She came up to me and said: "Can we talk?" I replied that I thought it reasonable that we should be able to do that. She said: "Why don't they grow up? Why don't they understand that we expect Parliament to operate effectively and efficiently?" I said that I had certainly raised that matter on a number of occasions as had others. She said that it was sad for the country that we are not seeing the right kind of behaviour.
By behaviour, I do not mean behaviour in the sense that people are misbehaving. However, we are not getting the kind of management in Parliament that we ought to have. The woman went on to ask me if I would raise the matter in the House, and I said that I most certainly would, and 1 have. It is important that we leave the right impression with the public, and we are not leaving that impression at the moment.
It is sad that part of the reason we face this so often is the inability of the Government to bring forward a legislative program at a time when it can be given the careful consideration that it deserves. I say to this Government, as I said to the previous Government that it is wrong to put complex taxation legislation before Parliament in the last three weeks prior to the end of the year and expect that parliamentarians will be able to give it the kind of careful consideration it must have in order to ensure that people do not have foisted upon them legislation that is inadequate.
It is not the preserve of the Government to decide whether or not legislation is adequate. Parliament is structured in such a way as to have Government put forward its proposals so that Parliament can then deal with those proposals. Parliament must be given sufficient time to deal with legislation in the depth necessary to come to grips with the complexities of tax changes. That is impossible for us if the Government and its advisers cannot bring legislation forward within a short period of time.

Mr. Speaker, the situation is very difficult for Members of Parliament and Canadian citizens. This bill is very complex. We must change the system immediately.
In the future, the Government should make its proposals and introduce its programs immediately after the Budget. [English]
I believe that it is necessary for the Government to have its legislative program ready for introduction immediately after

the budget debate. That is when we should be dealing with taxation legislation. 1 believe that it is not unreasonable to suggest to the Government that it should now embark upon a new system, a system which, out of necessity, should make the point with the civil servants who prepare both the Budget and the legislation that flows from it that legislation must be brought to Parliament within a maximum time of four weeks of the budget debate. The reason we are having to deal with time allocation today is that we did not get what we ought to have received early enough in the year.
I would like to go further by saying that it is not solely the responsibility of Government to manage the time of the House of Commons. When one manages the time of the House of Commons, one manages the time of all of its Members. It is therefore the responsibility of all of us to priorize the program of Government and to attempt wherever possible to move it forward, and to oppose it where opposition is necessary and desirable. It becomes therefore everyone's responsibility to pay particular attention to the over-all program the Government hopes to put forward and to work out a system among ourselves for dealing with that program. We cannot do that if we get the program in dribs and drabs. We cannot do that if we get the Budget in April and the taxation legislation that flows from it in December. How are we going to manage the time of Parliament if that is to be the case?
I hope, come the next session of Parliament beginning some time in the early part of 1986, that the Government will pay some heed to what I am suggesting. The legislation, if there is any, that flows from the Throne Speech should take no more than a month to introduce, and the legislation that flows from the Budget should not only be introduced immediately but should be dealt with forthwith. We ought not to be continually put in the situation in which we have been put over the many, many years of having to cram through at the last minute important, intricate, delicate legislation just because the Government or its advisers did not see the urgency of the matter and did not understand the complexity of the parliamentary system well enough to bring legislation forward in time to allow it to be dealt with.
This legislation can have and likely will have a detrimental effect on a large number of Canadians. How are they going to put their views before Parliament? How much time will there be for a committee to deal with this legislation given its diversity? How will people who have studied it have time to bring their concerns before the Parliament of Canada given that we are now entering the pre-Christmas season at which time the majority of people are already tied up with other important matters? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I would like to speak to the motion for allotting a limited period of time for subsequent consideration of the second reading stage of Bill C-84. As we know, the purpose of this Bill is to amend the Income Tax Act and related statutes and to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, the Financial Administration Act and the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act. This Bill is one of the major elements in the Government's strategy for injecting new vigour into the Canadian economy, hence the Government's emphasis on this legislation and the need for introducing a motion aimed at expediting its passage.
This Bill contains measures proposed in two Notices of Ways and Means Motions tabled in the House earlier this year, one a general Ways and Means Motion tabled on May 23 and the other a detailed Notice of a Ways and Means Motion tabled on November 21. The Bill is an integral component of a comprehensive strategy to secure durable economic growth and create jobs for all Canadians, and the Government's purpose in presenting this Bill is to provide a stable and consistent framework that will secure durable economic renewal. The major principles and broad parameters of this strategy were previously the subject of a clear and specific message when the Agenda for Economic Renewal was released in November 1984, and the first important measures were introduced when the Budget was brought down in May 1985.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the results are already being felt. The present rate of inflation is the lowest ever since 1971, and interest rate levels are such that major projects can now be undertaken. Of course the Opposition does not mention this, Mr. Speaker.
Since the Government came to office, the Canadian economy's performance has restored the faith of families and businesses in this country, and that is not being mentioned either. Economic growth has been far more vigorous than expected. Today, more than 300,000 Canadians who, a year ago, were unemployed have jobs. Consumer purchases, housing starts and investment are showing tremendous progress. The unemployment rate is still a little high but is dropping steadily, for the first time in ten years. This Bill marks a decisive stage in continuing our progress along the path we took on September 4, and its impact will undoubtedly be enhanced by the strategy already in place.
The Bill amends the Income Tax Act in significant ways, including a capital gains tax exemption of $500,000 that will encourage investment and enterpreneurship, although the Opposition prefers to take a distorted view of this measure. They cannot understand we are trying to work with and for Canadians. They cannot understand why a lifetime capital gains tax exemption of $500,000 is beneficial to business, to Canadians and especially to small businesses. Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak today on second reading of Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act and related statutes. This Bill is part of our Government's plan to facilitate lasting economic renewal by improving tax fairness, controlling and reducing high deficits and stimulating private initiative. Its passage will provide the legislative authority for several changes to income tax measures outlined in last May's Budget.
Changes that will encourage private initiative will include $500,000 personal capital gains exemption, measures to encourage RRSP and labour and pension fund investment in small business, improvements to tax incentives available for research and development, and a special tax credit for investment in Cape Breton.
Changes to improve Government effectiveness include an increase of $140 in the child tax credit and increased tax assistance for the disabled and artists. I can empathize with both those areas, Mr. Speaker, and I will expand on that in a moment. Furthermore, there are clear limits on Revenue Canada's powers of search and seizure.
Changes that will help to control the deficit include modifications to personal income tax indexation, an end to the
Time Allocation
federal tax reduction and an end to the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan.
The complexities of this Bill are obvious. Therefore, I urge the House to refer Bill C-84 to a legislative committee quickly, where it may be carefully and thoroughly examined.
Today, I would like to focus on the legislative changes that will aid artists, charities, small businesses and, time permitting, to examine the special investment tax credit.
Bill C-84 includes two measures that will aid the arts sector. Visual artists will be permitted to write off costs involved in creating a work of art in the year that the expenses are incurred. At present, they must wait until the work is sold. This alteration remedies the current rule that has caused difficulties for artists in valuing their finished works of art on hand, incurred expenses and the carrying of inventories for long periods of time.
This change will allow artists to write off the costs of creating art when they are incurred rather than when the art is sold and, very important, it will defer taxes in respect of the artistic endeavour until the artist realizes proceeds from the sale of his or her art. I believe that that is a tremendous change that will be applauded by artists across the country.
The second measure will permit an individual visual artist who donates his or her own work of art to charity after 1984 to elect any amount up to the fair market value of the work, as both the artist's proceeds of disposition and the amount of the gift. The current requirement has created an obstacle to giving by artists because the income inclusion often exceeds the 20 per cent limitation on the general charitable donation deduction and the gift can consequently cost the artist a substantial amount of money. This amendment alleviates the disincentive since an elected amount which is less than the fair market value of the gift will mean a smaller income inclusion and a greater use of the charitable donation deduction. This piece of legislation includes two measures of relevance to registered charities.
The first measure will permit registered charities, in the 1985 and subsequent taxation years, to engage in non-partisan political activities that are incidental to their primary charitable purposes or activities.
The amendment recognizes that it is appropriate for a charity to use its resources, within defined limits, for incidental political activities in support of its charitable goals. These activities would include advertising, rental of facilities or mass mailings to influence public opinion toward the organization's views on matters of law or Government policy related to its charitable purposes. I emphasize that it has to be related to the charitable purposes of that organization. Furthermore, this measure does not affect the present unrestricted ability of charity to provide information and express its views in briefs to Government to effect change in laws or policies.
The second measure concerns the donation of intangible capital property, such as shares, to charity. Currently, a taxpayer who donates tangible capital property to a charity is permitted under a present rule to elect to have an amount less

December 5, 1985
Time Allocation
than fair market value treated as both his or her proceeds and the amount of his or her gift. Bill C-84 will extend this special rule to donations of intangible capital property made after 1984 and will remove the requirement that the property be suitable for use by the charity directly in its activities.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stated in his Budget speech, lack of access to start-up capital has been a constraint for many small and medium sized businesses. Our Government is taking strong steps to remedy this situation.
At present, farmers and small businesses can arrange financing of up to $500,000 under the small business bonds program, at interest rates that have typically been 5 to 6 percentage points less than they would otherwise have had to pay.
The small business bonds program was scheduled to expire in 1985. It has played a useful role in providing interest rate relief in cases where a business failure might otherwise have resulted. The program has been particularly important to agriculture and there is a growing awareness of its role in that sector.
Bill C-84 will extend the program for a further two years to cover debt instruments issued before the end of 1987. Bill C-84 also introduces measures which will allow taxpayers who have borrowed under this program to either refinance existing loans or obtain new loans at any time before 1988 where the borrowers are in financial difficulty.
Moreover, the present rules provide that the aggregate face value of all such bonds issued by the taxpayer and other related parties cannot exceed $500,000. The measures contained in this legislation ensure that a taxpayer in financial difficulty may issue a small business bond at any time after May 23, 1985, and before 1988 if the total principal amounts outstanding does not exceed $500,000.
The last measure 1 would like to mention briefly is the special investment tax credit. Five years ago a tax credit was introduced to encourage investment in areas of Canada suffering from high unemployment and low per-capita income. This tax credit was scheduled to expire on December 31 of this year. Bill C-84 extends the expiry date for one year to accommodate investments made on or before December 31, 1986. A further extension of the credit applies for buildings under construction on December 31, 1986. In such cases, the tax credit will be available if the property is acquired before 1988.
In conclusion, I move:
That, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 9(4)(a), the House continue to sit through the lunch hour for the purpose of continuing its consideration of the motion now before it.

Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) and others, could use their allotted time to explain why, under what rationale, and how they can claim on the one hand that they are fighting the deficit and, on the other hand, that they are giving away some $5 billion in fiscal benefits. In my view, they should do that. I think you should explain why. And the Conservatives could also explain why, when they are so anxious to fight the deficit, they grant benefits to the rich, why they give close to $9 billion in benefits to the multinational oil companies.
Perhaps we could be told about that, and clearly nine hours of debate have not been enough because nobody has referred to that. Certainly there are measures the Conservatives would want to brag about more, and we have nothing against that. But in the Opposition, we believe our duty is to point to the weaknesses in any legislation. We know very well the majority will revel in the strong points, but go ahead, discuss them, tell the Canadian taxpayers by way of this debate why you are going to increase taxes, why you are going to deindex income

tax tables, which will be costing taxpayers an extra $11 billion. Yes, you tell us! speechtext:
The Hon. Member should ask me to go easy. This is a record that is worthy of further exposure and further examination.
This Government stated that it was going to do a lot better than that. We might categorize the improvement in the gesture of a well-known if not well-loved international leader as being a tiny little bit. That is all it is. For the Government to be introducing after such a short period of debate, barely into double figures in terms of hours, a measure which has such far-reaching impact-the Government says it is for the betterment, but we know, having done the calculations, that it will have far-reaching impact for the worst for the majority of Canadians-that it should have the nerve to introduce a motion of closure after barely double figures of hours of debate in this Chamber, does not reflect very well on this Government's stated commitment to consultation. First and foremost, it is in this Chamber that the consultation that the Government trumpeted so loudly should be taking place.
It is unfortunate that the Government has shown that it too is having difficulty in managing a parliamentary agenda. It is particularly unfortunate when we consider the very housekeeping nature, I would not use the word "trivial", but the fairly basic and simple nature of some of the legislation that has been put before us, that the lack of management of the parliamentary agenda should have led us to this point where we are debating closure of Bill C-84 which essentially enshrines the major Government budget measures in legislation. Just the size of Bill C-84 surely is illustrative of the importance the Government should give it in debate in this House. Just the thickness of that bill should give us an indication that it is something to be taken seriously and exposed to broad and far-reaching and, yes, let us not be afraid to use the word, lengthy public discussion in this Chamber.
When I look at the nature of some of the amendments, I have to acknowledge that they are worth while. Indeed, in my speech on the Bill I stated that if 1 was not able to say something good, I would not say anything at all. I mentioned that there were worth-while measures. We saw another one put before us yesterday. Of course, we have not had the opportunity to analyse it sufficiently. Again, it was a sign of some common sense in the tax system. The good effect of that common sense, 1 am afraid, is very much negatived by the bite
December 5, 1985

which Bill C-84 proposes to take out of the pockets of ordinary Canadians. I was surprised to hear the use of that phrase criticized by a Member of parliament quite recently in the debate on Bill C-84 because I think most ordinary Canadians know that they are ordinary Canadians. They can tell when they come to do their income tax form not only where they stand in the relative strata of income in our society-where the top 10 per cent takes 40 per cent of the income and the bottom 20 per cent takes 4 per cent-they know where they stand and where they will be standing after this Government's Budget. It is not going to be in a position of relative advantage to where they stood before that Budget.
The proposal to take away the indexing provisions from the tax bans in the present income tax system, to cut out the first 3 per cent, can best be characterized as profiteering on inflation. If there is one thing on which the previous Liberal Government could be complimented, it is that it did have the intelligence to realize in the early 1970s that inflation was supplementing or swelling Government revenues to a degree that was inordinate. Inflation was taking too much out of the pockets of individual Canadian taxpayers. The Government of the time realized that those taxes should be indexed in order that the effect of inflation on income would not lead to an excess tax burden when considering taxation in relation to disposable taxable income.
I am afraid to say that that approach is now going by the boards. The deduction of 3 per cent from the indexing provisions means that we will be in the position that we were in before 1973 of the Government making a profit on inflation. I do not think that is progressive nor is it the sort of provision that we want to see in our tax system. I for one would like to see the House spend much more time debating that sort of measure.
Yesterday we heard the Government's announcement on the alternative minimum tax. I think it would be worth while to take a few minutes to juxtapose the effect that will have on the effect of the changes in the pension deduction limits particularly on those with higher incomes. When the Registered Retirement Savings Plan and Registered Pension Plan deductions combined reach the level of $15,500 in 1990, we can anticipate that far from the cut-off point today of someone who earns an average income of $50,000, Canadians earning up to $200,000 will have the opportunity through contributing to pension plans of sheltering as big a portion of their income as those making a contribution of $1,200 or $1,500 per year for a much more modest pension. I would like to put on the record the effect that this will have on earnings that are far from modest but not by any means the highest.
Before the Budget, someone earning an income of $80,000 per year would have protected through his pension contribution that which was allowable for the deduction and would have saved $1,761 in taxes. After the Budget, by 1990 they will be able to save $4,328 in taxes. These are figures put together by the National Council on Welfare, the contribution
Time Allocation
of which we acknowledge. That represents a very considerable increase in the tax break on RRSPs and RPPs. I do not say that that is necessarily bad. I do say that there must be further discussion on this sort of measure. This is the sort of thing that is worthy of detailed consideration because that $2,500 would make up a very substantial proportion of the income of a person on welfare. In fact, under the welfare regime in the Province of Quebec, I believe that that would pay for the welfare of a single person under 30. While those amounts may seem to those of us who are fortunate to have reasonably high incomes to be modest figures, they are in fact very significant figures when related to the other social goals and objectives to which we in this Party certainly subscribe and for which the Government has expressed support, support which we do not see in practical terms.
When I rose to speak in the debate the other day, I spoke at some length on capital gains. I heard my colleague, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), quote from the report of the Financial Post, from which I too had quoted, concerning the way in which the $500,000 capital gains exemption could be used. Since I last spoke, other examples have appeared in the newspapers of the way in which these tax loopholes may be used.
We heard of the example of a research tax credit that was being converted into Brazilian cruzeiros in order that the people who were investing the money could presumably profit from the forecast fall in the value of that unfortunate country's currency. That is but one example. I am sure there will be many other examples of ways in which present tax loopholes and the newly introduced capital gains exemption can be misused. That is why I feel that Bill C-84 deserves a lot more debate than the Government is prepared to allow.

speechtext:
Once again, Mr. Speaker, we find ourselves in a situation where the Government with its huge majority decides to gag the Opposition. It is disquieting to note that this is not an isolated case. On the contrary, if we examine the Government record over the past year, this is the sixth time the Government resorts to Standing Order 80 to silence the Opposition and avoid a serious debate on important measures.
The first time the Government used this tactic was on Bill C-15, the Investment Canada Act. Then came Bill C-62, the employment equity legislation. As we recall, that particular Bill was badly drafted, it did not include any kind of enforcement mechanism, a Bill which was discredited by all the designated groups which were supposed to benefit from it.
After that we had Bill C-70 with its cut-backs and deindexation of family allowances: the Government chose to drop the guillotine, gag the Opposition and get the House to pass quickly that despicable Bill to which most Canadians are opposed. Then in turn came Bill C-80, the excise tax on drugs sold over the counter, the tax on all kinds of health products about which the public has again voiced strong opposition. The

December 5, 1985
Time Allocation
Government also ended the debate as soon as possible by imposing closure on the House of Commons with respect to Bill C-86 which will enable the Government to re-imburse the major depositors of the Canadian Commercial Bank and of the Northland Bank, people having deposits in excess of $60,000 which are not covered under deposit insurance. Again the public raised hell, so the Government imposed closure to silence the Opposition.
Here we are today with Bill C-84, a rather special piece of legislation. A simple look reveals that the Bill has 234 pages, 143 clauses, then a schedule with 11 more clauses. It is almost an encyclopaedia, Mr. Speaker, a telephone directory, a Sears catalogue, a Bill thick enough to make Government backbenchers understand our position. Indeed, as we hear in the TV commercial, "there is no need for a dictionary to understand that". It is a huge Bill which will affect every facet of taxation. The Government lowers the boom, not after two or three weeks of debates, but barely after two days, even before the end of the second day of debate. Earlier today my colleague from Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) said after nine hours of debate, if Hon. Members want to know, I checked with the Table officials. We had discussed the principles of this bill for exactly nine hours and 45 minutes when the Government decided to put an end to the debate. I am beginning to understand why. The more I look at this bill, the more I realize that it does not involve only one principle. There are 25 principles involved, as the bill affects many provisions of many acts including, naturally, the Income Tax Act, but also the Canada Pension Plan, the Unemployment Insurance Act, the Financial Administration Act and the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act.
It is therefore a very complex bill, and I believe that the reason why this Government wants to ram this measure through the House of Commons is that it includes atrocious proposals, the worst one being the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption that will benefit the rich. Naturally, this proposal has been hidden in this Bill. It has been burried with some 50 others. The Bill includes 69 proposals. We have spoken about the others and I can tell you all about them. Personal exemptions are being de-indexed. This is an underhand way to collect taxes without anyone taking notice. Deductions for dependent children will be reduced. All these proposals are hidden in this Bill. Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Members opposite do not want to hear the truth and that is why they have imposed closure. Indeed, that is why the Government uses closure more and more.
We have a Government which uses its enormous majority to force its views on the Opposition. Instead of being content to win one vote after another in the House of Commons, the Government wants to prevent the Opposition from having reasonable discussions about its legislation.
This Bill is so far-reaching that there can be no justification for cutting off debate after only nine hours and 25 minutes. It is unthinkable, Mr. Speaker.
A Canadian Press article had this to say:
It is a real disgrace. The Government is steamrolling the Bill.
[ Translation]
This means that the Government is ramming the Bill through the House of Commons. It is exactly what is happening.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to express my serious concern about the use of time allocation with respect to the measure which is before us. Last night those of us who stayed in this place quite late in the evening had a moving experience in talking about parliamentary reform. We had hoped that, perhaps, we could work together in a more positive way in the House to benefit all Canadians. Again, today, we have not only time allocation imposed but the fact that the debate will take up the lunch hour is symbolic.
I wish to concentrate my remarks pertaining to Bill C-84 on the social aspects of it. I wish to deal with the effects the Bill will have on child and family benefits. The Bill which reflects the Conservative Budget is really the beginning of a process of erosion with respect to family benefits generally. I wish to illustrate this point with several examples. It is not just I and my Party who say that this measure is a serious erosion of family benefits, it is all the social policy groups in Canada which have appeared both before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs and the legislative committee to which Bill C-70 was referred. There was not one witness who appeared before either committee who agreed with the measures being taken by the Government.
The combined package of tax changes which will affect the child tax credit, the child tax exemption and the family allowance is definitely an attack on families and children. In
December 5, 1985

particular, it is an attack on women. I have said this before in relation to the family allowance issue. I say it now in relation to the changes and supposed reforms which are now before us. In my view they are not at all reforms to tax measures in a positive sense but something which will really hurt families.
I would like to remind Hon. Members that we are talking about not just average families who have to pay the costs of raising children and who have many more expenses and responsibilities than taxpayers who have no children at all, but we are talking about families which have several children and who are hurt several times over by the tax changes which will reduce benefits for families with children.
I would like to remind Members of the House about the very high incidence of poor families in Canada. The number is not decreasing in my Province of British Columbia. In fact, it is increasing. It increased 400 per cent over the last four years in British Columbia. There are over 4.4 million poor still in Canada and there are 1.5 million poor children. We hear these figures but I hope Hon. Members will take a moment really to comprehend what they mean.
We have already spoken about the family allowance which will be deindexed by 3 per cent. We will continue to protest this move. We have petitions flooding into our offices every day protesting such a cut. This is a measure which, by 1990, will take away $1 billion from the children of Canada. It will reduce the value of the family allowance, the only universal program which goes to all families. When representatives of the CLC appeared before the legislative committee they said that in 20 years' time, by the year 2005, the family allowance will actually decrease in value from $32, which it is today, to $18. That is a substantial decrease. If one thinks of the effect that this will have on families with several children, it can be seen that it is a major erosion in terms of the universal family program.
Of course, with regard to the Bill which is before us we are referring to tax measures. In this respect let us consider the child tax credit. We will agree, as will all the authorities, that this is a progressive tax measure. It is targeted at the low and middle income families in society. At any rate, it has been that in the past and according the Conservative Government it is really a program that is in place to help those in greatest need. The Government professes to be focusing on improving the child tax credit while it reduces other benefits to children. If we look at the measure before us more closely we will see that even the child tax credit, which will be increased next year, will be reduced in the long run. I would like to be more specific in this respect.
As I have said, the child tax credit will be increased by about $70 next year. I would like to point out that this increase will be cancelled by the sales taxes which the Budget will impose on these same families. Thus, poor families will not really have any more in their pockets. The amount of money will increase to $454 per child by the year 1987.
However, let us remember that the Conservative Government while pretending to give with the one hand is actually taking away with the other hand through the deindexation of
Time Allocation
the child tax credit. It will be reduced considerably. There will be a cap placed on the cost of living index with respect to the child tax credit by the year 1989. The eligibility requirements for the child tax credit are being seriously reduced. To qualify for the child tax credit this year a family will have to earn $26,500, which is just getting close to the average income. We would rather see that figure set at $30,000. However, the eligibility requirement is being reduced to $23,500. That might not sound like a big reduction in one year but if the deindexation is added to the level of the child tax credit the eligibility goes down year after year after year.
Let us listen to what the CLC had to say with respect to the child tax credit. It says that by the year 2005, in 20 years, the value of the child tax credit as a result of the measures in this Bill will be reduced to $326. It is projected that it will go down from $480 in 1988 to $384 by the year 2005.
Not only is the value of the child tax credit decreasing but the eligibility requirements are being drastically reduced. Families earning $13,800 will mark the eligibility level for the child tax credit in 20 years' time. That is down from $26,000. Even the poorest families will not be receiving the child tax credit by that time. This is something that is extremely serious. It is dishonest and hypocritical of the Government to say that the tax measures it is bringing in will benefit those in greatest need. It will not benefit those in greatest need. Instead, it will penalize them.
The National Council on Welfare says that by the year 1990 even the poorest families will lose $8 just in specific family benefits. And if you add all the other measures in the Budget, they will suffer even more. But that is reflective of Tory philosophy. There is no question about that. It is a philosophy which leads to finding $1 billion overnight to bail out the banks, at the same time taking $1 million away from Canada's children by 1990. It gives $9 billion to the oil companies and takes away the benefits from families. It is incredible that the Government can say that it is interested in strengthening families and in helping those in greatest need. These measures do not help families. In fact, they are very harmful to families and reflect the true philosophy of the Tories. They do not really care about people and families, particularly those people who are hardest hit.
We feel that the minimum tax is a step in the right direction, but is only a step, let us not kid ourselves. It has not erased the errors imposed on us by the Liberal Government. We feel we should reduce the marginal tax rate to the 1981 benefits. If we did this, we would have lots of money to improve family benefits, to increase employment programs and to reindex the family allowance. We would gain over $1.7 billion in revenue just this year if we went back to the 1981 marginal tax levels.
Even with the minimum tax, we will have money coming in which I believe should be used to do away with the deindexation of the child tax credit and the family allowance.

I have just a short time left to mention the child tax exemption. This is a very regressive measure. We said over and over in committee that this should be done away with, but only if we increase the child tax credit to cover the average and middle income families, and only if we maintain a fully indexed family allowance. The Government has not had the guts to do much for the child tax exemption. It will reduce it gradually by 1989 to the same amount as the family allowance. It will be deindexed as well.
Here again, this is an attack on taxpayers who have children. It is causing them to contribute, whereas those families who do not have children are not contributing in the same way. It is the middle income families which are hardest hit by these measures.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would very much like the opportunity to debate Bill C-84 but I am precluded from doing so because of the motion of closure which was moved by this Conservative Government. As a duly elected Member of this House, I would submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that I have a right to speak to the merits of this particular piece of legislation in order for my constituents, and others, to understand and appreciate where I stand and where the Liberal Opposition stands on this important piece of legislation. However, I am precluded from doing so because of this shameful, undemocratic motion put forward by the Conservative Government.
This is the sixth time since Parliament began a year ago that the Government has found it necessary to invoke closure, notwithstanding the fact that when that Party was on this side of the House it cried foul on the rare occasions in which the former administration invoked closure. The Conservative Government is showing contempt for every Hon. Member of this House. It is showing contempt for the democratic process and for Parliament. We have had only nine short hours of debate on a piece of legislation which implements the major budget measures which were introduced last May.
One could ask why this Government has decided to invoke closure after only nine hours of debate. Why is this Government so hypocritical when it comes to the issues of closure? I think the answer is obvious, and I am sure you would agree with me, Mr. Speaker, when I say that the Government is doing so because it is embarrassed. It is because it cannot stand the heat of the criticism arising out of its Budget of last May. Hon. Members of the Conservative Party cannot stand up in this House and defend this Bill, so what did they do? They decided to cut off debate and preclude Hon. Members of this House from speaking to the merits of this particular piece of legislation.
When I say that my privileges are being breached, I am speaking for all other Hon. Members of this House who want to speak to this piece of legislation but who cannot, and it is a shameful situation. It shows the arrogance of this Government and the hypocrisy.
The people of Canada spoke on September 4 of last year. They clearly wanted a change and they got that change. They
elected 211 Conservative Members of Parliament. But they also elected 70 opposition Members and one independent. The people of Canada did not elect a dictatorship, nor did they expect that a dictatorship would result. By invoking closure on this occasion, and on the five other occasions, the Government is leading Canadians to conclude that this Conservative Government would like to rule Canada as a dictatorship. The Opposition Party is essential. It is a check and balance that this Government, or any other Government, does not run rough-shod over the people of Canada. Why is this Government stifling debate on this particular piece of legislation? Why has it done so on five previous occasions, which I indicated is unparliamentary and undemocratic? It is the basis of a parliamentary system that the Opposition be heard but, more importantly, that it be given an opportunity to debate in this House items of concern to Canadians. What has happened is that closure is becoming the rule rather than the exception to the rule. All Hon. Members recognize that closure is a tool which may be necessary in certain circumstances. I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that those circumstances are extreme circumstances when, for whatever reason, a piece of legislation must be passed and passed expeditiously. Closure is not meant, and was never meant, to be a tool used by Government to stifle healthy, constructive debate in this House. But that is precisely what the Government is doing with this piece of legislation.
This Parliament and our democracy can only work with a healthy and vigorous Opposition. Had it not been for the Opposition, the Government would not have backed down on issues like the deindexation of senior citizens' pensions. It was because of the work done by the Opposition in this House and in mobilizing public support for the position taken by the Opposition, that the Government eventually backed down. We had a healthy debate, a good debate, on the issue of deindexation of senior citizens' pensions. The Government realized that it had erred and it backed down.
All we are asking for now is the opportunity for Members on this side of the House to speak on Bill C-84. However, we cannot do that because the Government is using its overwhelming majority to cut off debate. It would not take long to give every Member of the House an opportunity to speak for 10 or 20 minutes on Bill C-84. In that way the Government could avoid being criticized for bringing in closure. However, the Government has decided to drop the guillotine on the Opposition members.
What is worse, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that the Government is thinking of proroguing Parliament. It is obvious that the reason the Government is thinking of doing that is that it is without direction. It does not know where it is going. It realizes that its legislative agenda is stale. Yet, it wants to prorogue Parliament and give its Members a two-month vacation, but it refuses to allow members of the Opposition an opportunity to debate important pieces of legislation.
December 5, 1985

There is also a suggestion that the Conservative Government wants to extend the Christmas break by two weeks. I call that shameful. We could be here debating important pieces of legislation. I invite the Government, rather than extending the Christmas break, to restrict it in order to give members of the Opposition an opportunity to debate this piece of legislation. I want the opportunity to articulate the reasons why-you are about to cut me off, Mr. Speaker. You have indicated that I have one minute left in this very important debate. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that you would be an accessory to this shameful act if you cut me off. I do not intend to sit down of my own accord. You are going to have to cut me off when my time expires on this particular motion. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that you are being an accessory to this unparliamentary action by the Conservative Government.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF JOB LOSSES AT CN REPAIR SHOPS IN MONCTON-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
1 should like to call the attention of the House on the uncertainty which exists among working men and women at the CN workshops in Moncton, New Brunswick. These employees are aware that CN is currently reviewing its maintenance services and they fear that final recommendation to the Federal Government will be to close the Moncton workshops. The result would be a direct loss of 1,200 jobs. Already, Mr. Speaker, the CN has announced that it was laying off 225 workers.
On October 9, in reply to a question of mine, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) indicated that the lay-offs in Moncton were the result of reduced railway traffic and wished that these lay-offs were only temporary. How does the Minister explain the fact that 140 of these employees have been notified that their dismissal is permanent?
So far, the Government has neither taken a firm stand nor assured the workers that it would preserve these jobs in Moncton.
Although these employees are disappointed and very concerned, it is with determination that they intend to continue to fight for the Government to preserve these jobs.

subsubtopic: CN MARINE-AWARDING OF FERRY CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is no secret that the Canadian shipbuilding industry is in dire straits, to say the least. Because of the huge deficit inherited by the Government, government assistance has been minimized and this could close down or eliminate much of the shipbuilding industry in Canada.
How can our industry compete with other countries which give their shipbuilding industries massive subsidies, including concessionary financing and selling below cost? It is totally unrealistic to expect the Canadian shipbuilding industry to compete with predatory prices from abroad. There is no free market in shipbuilding in the world today.
A moratorium on foreign-built ships and offshore platforms and rigs being brought into Canadian registry is imperative for the survival of the shipbuilding industry.
Governments after Governments have urged Canadians to buy Canadian. This must apply as well to the Government to buy Canadian ships made by Canadian taxpayers.

subsubtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCE-LETTER FROM SINGLE PARENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand a letter from a constituent of mine in Aspen Park, British Columbia. It reads in part as follows:
I am a single parent with 3 children-I have been the sole supporter of these children for 8'/2 years.
I get $870.00 per month from Human Resources, plus the family allowance.
I pay $465 per month for rent, which is more than I can afford on Welfare.
My point in all this-is that I think it would really do us in if I lost the family allowance. We would not have enough money for groceries if that happened.
I would like Mr. Mulroney ... and many others in their financial category to try to live on less than $1,000 per month and look after 4 people on that amount like I am doing. I would be willing to bet they couldn't make it.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the important tax measure announced yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in the form of a minimum tax for individuals earning over $50,000. The House will recall that in 1983, 7,036 Canadian taxpayers who had incomes of over $50,000 managed to pay not a cent of income tax, thanks to all kinds of tax deductions.
Mr. Speaker, that is the kind of inequity and injustice Canadians were condemning. They asked for amendments to the Income Tax Act to close this loophole.
Mr. Speaker, this is now being done, and let me tell you I consulted with Canadians whose incomes were over $50,000. "We agree with the principle", they said, "and it is entirely
fair and normal that Canadians should pay a minimum tax . .." Those were their own words.
Our Government is on the right track with this measure, which is the kind of change Canadians have been asking us to implement. It was unacceptable that the rich could avoid paying income tax, and I want to remind Canadians that it was the Government opposite, the previous Government, that made this possible. We have put a stop to that now, and our new tax measure which is more equitable, will involve a minimum tax of between 24 and 27 per cent and collect $300 million for the federal treasury.

subsubtopic: STIFFER PENALTIES FOR DRUNKEN DRIVERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-19 is tough. That is the message we want Canadians to understand about the new drinking and driving laws which came into effect yesterday, December 4. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) visits cities across the country over the next 10 days to publicize these new laws, let all Canadians be aware of the new, tough penalties for impaired driving; fines up to $300 for a first offence and a minimum of three months' suspension from driving, mandatory jail terms and much longer suspensions for second offences.
This legislation has had unprecedented public support from community groups such as MADD and PRIDE who have led the way, police, doctors, and even the distillers themselves. Only with tough penalties can we hope to reduce dramatically the tragedy and high costs of the loss of human life and suffering now caused by individuals who drink and drive.
Yes, as we approach the Christmas season, Canadians have much to rejoice about, but if you have had a drink to celebrate, stop. Before you go to your car, think. Do you want to face the costs of the fine, the increased insurance rates, the fallout of having your licence suspended and a possible jail term? Act, as this Government has done; please, don't drink and drive.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Yesterday the Minister of Finance introduced his minimum tax proposal. He indicated that in the calculation of their tax payable, upper-income earners would get a $40,000 automatic deduction. subsubtopic: INTRODUCTION OF MINIMUM TAX-DEDUCTION FOR UPPER-INCOME EARNERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in designing this tax I looked very closely at the proposal that was put forward by the New Democratic Party as one of the elements that we analysed. If the Hon. Member would think carefully, he would understand that under their proposal, which said that anybody earning over $50,000 would be taxed 20 per cent on total income, he would see that that means that someone who is not paying any tax who earns $49,999 would pay no tax. A person earning $50,000 would pay $10,000 worth of tax on that additional $1 worth of income. I do not think that is fair, and I am sure the Hon. Member does not either.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance is playing a bit of a shell game. Our proposal was anything but what he has indicated. We felt that everyone should pay their fair share no matter what their level of income.
Would the Minister explain why he has included a carry forward provision in his proposal when he knows that even Ronald Reagan felt that it was inappropriate for the American minimum tax proposal? Why does the Minister allow people to roll ahead their tax deductions up to seven years if they cannot use them in one year now that there is a minimum tax?

Mr. Speaker, on July 29, 1984, the NDP Leader called for a 20 per cent minimum tax on the incomes of those Canadians earning over $50,000. That is the proposal to which I was referring, and I think the Hon. Member should consider that proposal carefully when he reflects on his first question.
The reason for the carry forward is quite clear. There are a number of very valid social and economic objectives that are encouraged through the Income Tax Act. We do not feel that this minimum tax should be used to discourage that type of activity in the social and economic policy sphere. It is for that reason that we have allowed for a carry forward so that those incentives are not lost forever by those who will be asked to pay a minimum tax.
