speakeroldname: Hon. Michel Cote (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Canada Post) moved:
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Canada Post Corporation; Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
That Bill C-84, to amend the Tax Rebate Discounting Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs I am very pleased to be able to take the floor today and introduce Bill C-83, an Act to amend the Tax Rebate Discounting Act.
For the benefit of those who might not be too familiar with the tax rebate discounting practice, I would say that it enables a taxpayer who expects a tax refund to go to a discounter who will prepare his return and pay him cash on the basis of the expected refund.

I am proud, Mr. Speaker, to be able to tell Members of the House that the measures we are proposing will remove the abuses that have grown up in this field. At the same time, consumers who want and need the services will be able to make a free and informed choice. Some have suggested outlawing the service entirely, Mr. Speaker. The Government has
rejected this option. Even though that would have been very popular in some quarters, we firmly believe that Canadians should have the right to make such decisions and choices for themselves. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, they also have the right to be protected, and the measures I am proposing will ensure that low-income Canadians are not victimized by unscrupulous practices.
At this point I would like to summarize the main features of our comprehensive package of reforms. First, Bill C-83 will lower the maximum rate discounters can charge. Second, the Bill will provide for tougher enforcement and better administration. Third, we propose periodic payments of the child tax credit. Fourth, we will encourage and assist financial institutions to provide alternatives for discounting. Finally, we will ensure that Canadian consumers are fully informed about discounting and alternative options.
These are the elements of our program and I am convinced that they are both practical and equitable. They will, as 1 intend to make clear, eliminate the disadvantages of tax discounting while retaining its advantages. In short, they are shaped by the Government's approach to the establishment and maintenance of an efficient, equitable market-place.
I want to stress that this package of measures was brought forward with the advice and active co-operation of my colleagues, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). I want to thank them in the House for their interest and support in this matter.
It is worth noting that although tax discounting has always been legal in Canada, the practice was not federally regulated until 1978 when the present Tax Rebate Discounting Act was passed. In 1979, the turn-around time for tax returns was 17 weeks. This has now been reduced by at least 50 per cent. Also, in 1979 only 7,000 people used the services of tax discounters. By this year the number of Canadians who have sold their tax refunds has grown to half a million. With so many Canadian consumers using the services of tax discounters, the Government wanted to ensure that their interests were being looked after in the best possible manner. As Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, I decided to review tax discounting and update our present legislation in order to deal with current realities and initiate a wide range of measures in order to address the practice of tax discounting in its entirety.
As I mentioned, the Government is proposing five initiatives. The first two are legislative and are addressed by the legislation now before the House.
First, a new rate structure on the maximum allowable rate charged by discounters will be put in place by Bill C-83. The rate charged on any portion of a refund over S300 will be limited to 5 per cent. The rate for the first $300 of a refund will be 15 per cent, which recognizes the fee charged for filling out the client's tax return.

December 5, 1985

Second, proposed revisions in Bill C-83 will improve the Government's capacity to administer, detect and prosecute violations of the Tax Rebate Discounting Act. For example, the time limit on prosecutions under the Act will be extended from the present six months to two years.
Third, measures will be introduced at a later date to provide for the periodic payment of the child tax credit. These measures will ensure that recipients receive a majority of their child tax credit payment before income tax returns are due and will thus virtually eliminate the need to discount the child tax credit.
Fourth, through simple administrative measures we will be making it easier for financial institutions such as credit unions and caisses populaires to offer alternatives to tax discounting. For example, such institutions could offer loans at normal consumer rates on the strength of expected tax refunds.
Finally, we will initiate and stress information programs so that consumers who choose to use discounters will know what is involved and what their options are.

As you know, Mr. Speaker, consultation has always been the hallmark of this Government, and the measures proposed to revise the tax rebate discounting practice are indeed the results of many wide-ranging consultations. Before making any decision, we have had consultations with provincial Governments, discounters, social service agencies, consumers' associations, businessmen, Members of Parliament, and the Canadian public at large. A working paper was published last June and a special conference was convened in August of this year. The question was also examined at the Federal-Provincial-Territorial Conference of Ministers of Consumer and Corporate Affairs held last September 10. Those consultations made it possible to reach a general consensus, namely that it was necessary to reform tax rebate discounting. For practically all parties involved, the statu quo was quite simply unacceptable. [English)
Undoubtedly, some will contend that the practice of tax discounting should have been abolished entirely. I am aware of the arguments for such a prohibition and I reject them. It is our considered view that Canadians must have the option of discounting money owed to them by way of any tax refund. To deny this kind of market choice to Canadians would have been unfair. Canadians should be free to choose discounting services if they want. The challenge was to reform tax discounting, eliminate the flaws in the way it is practised and leave a legitimate service in place. At the same time, we wanted to ensure that there was adequate protection for the consumer.
Likewise, it was argued that discounting of the child tax credit should have been prohibited. Again, our goal here is to prevent the diversion of child tax credit payments away from low income recipients. This will be done effectively and fairly through a periodic payment of the child tax credit rather than through a ban on discounting those credits.
Tax Rebate Discounting Act
From an administrative standpoint, such a ban would be impossible to define and enforce effectively. Because of the different types of tax credits under the present system, it was not clear what portion of the refund is a child tax credit. As well, such a ban would keep discounting legal except for those who appear to need it the most. That is precisely the kind of situation that leads to loan-sharking and rule bending.
Constant monitoring of complex laws and formulas would have been necessary. Even then, unscrupulous discounters who were faced with a demand for needy child tax credit recipients would have found ways to defeat the intent of the prohibition.
Furthermore, outlawing the discounting of the child tax credit would have made discounting available to all Canadians except low-income mothers. Imagine a child tax credit recipient going to a discounter and finding out, after her tax return had been prepared, that she could not discount the child tax credit. Instead of the large cheque which she expected, she would receive a bill of perhaps $30 for her tax return preparation. In my view, such discrimination cannot be justified.
Our solution is to pay the child tax credit periodically, thereby eliminating the need to discount the child tax credit.
Our approach has been to attack the cause of the problem rather than just its symptoms.

Thanks to the measures proposed in Bill C-83, Mr. Speaker, consumers will pay a lot less for the services of a tax rebate discounter. Under the new rates, the maximum a taxpayer will have to pay on a $1,000 reimbursement would be $80. These costs would include the preparation of the income tax return by the discounter. Under the previous rates, the consumers' cost was $150. This means savings of nearly 50 per cent. To set up this new rate, we have duly taken into account the limits imposed by the Criminal Code as well as the difference between a loan and a discount.

First, in contrast to normal lending practices, discounters prepare their client's tax returns. The fee for that service would normally vary from client to client but is always included in the discount rate. Second, when cash is advanced by a discounter there is no agreement on when the discounter will receive his or her money back. Therefore, a comparison to normal lending rates is difficult.
However, I would like to illustrate what will happen to such rates under Bill C-83. Assuming a turn-around time of eight weeks and a tax preparation value of $35 to $40, the discount rate proposed in Bill C-83 provides the equivalent annual rate of about 25 per cent to 30 per cent for a refund of $800. This rate is well below that in the current Act, and is also far below the criminal rate of 60 per cent. The discount rate proposed in Bill C-83 demonstrates a clear intention to rationalize discounting with the criminal law while appropriately accounting for the differences between lending and discounting.

December 5, 1985
Tax Rebate Discounting Act
Discounting is one alternative which consumers have to obtain needed cash. Other initiatives have been undertaken to make it easier for consumers to find alternative sources of immediate cash. 1 have mentioned that it will be easier for Canadians to get loans on the strength of their anticipated tax refunds. During our consultations, representatives of credit unions and caisses populaires told us that they would be willing to offer loans on tax refunds at normal consumer rates if there is enough demand within the community and enough co-operation and assistance from community organizations. These institutions themselves suggested a few administrative measures which could be put in place quite easily. For exem-ple, tax refund cheques could be sent directly to credit unions in repayment of loans, but not other correspondence which Revenue Canada might want to send to taxpayers. The Government will be taking such steps to help financial institutions to provide alternatives to tax discounting.
Some of the other items in the over-all reform package concern the provision of information. Freedom of choice works best when consumers can make informed decisions. We will provide facts about the true cost of discounting, alternatives to the practice, the availability of tax preparation assistance and the speed at which tax returns are normally processed. All these things should help consumers decide the options which are in their own best interest.
People should be aware that the turn-around time for receiving tax returns has decreased. I think there are many Canadians who, if made aware of this fact, would choose to wait what is now a relatively short period of time and claim their entire refund rather than go to tax discounters.

Mr. Speaker, many community groups are now helping people prepare their income tax returns and 1 believe that is true all across Canada.
They could easily share their experience with credit unions and caisses populaires and thus contribute to the good operation of the new loan programs.
Again, Mr. Speaker, we believe that Canadians should be able to make free and enlightened choices. Which means that they must have available all necessary information, and we have a responsibility in this regard.
We will therefore launch a dynamic information campaign, so that all Canadian families will receive information on tax discounting together with their January family allowance cheque. We shall also be contacting interested groups, so they may properly advise their members.
Also Revenue Canada will offer Canadian taxpayers all the information needed through its extensive system of regional offices. Finally, we will make extensive use of the media to reach the public at large.

Related to the issue of making sure that consumers are well informed, the revisions which we are proposing to the Act will also contain specific provisions to ensure that people who use
the services of discounters will be given all the information and documentation related to their transactions. In the past, people who used discounters often dropped off the relevant information, got their cash, and that was it. Some discounters even refused to give copies of the completed returns back to taxpayers. The new Act will require discounters to provide clients with copies of their tax returns and related information slips upon request. Furthermore, under Bill C-83, tax discounters will have a legal obligation to retain copies of all documents related to a discounting transaction. Thus, these will be available for examination by officials, if necessary.
It will also become an offence for a discounter to provide false information to a client or to an official. A common complaint which led to these measures was to the effect that the time limit on prosecutions under the present Tax Rebate Discounting Act was far too short. Indeed, in the past it was not unusual for suspicions to be raised about an unscrupulous discounter, only to have the time limit expire before the suspicions could be fully investigated. This will change, since Bill C-83 extends the time limit of prosecutions under the Act from six months to two years. In addition, the new Act permits income tax officials to disclose information necessary for enforcement to administrators of the Act.
In summation, the Government is presenting a complete package of initiatives to reform the practice of tax rebate discounting. Through Bill C-83 discounting will still be available but at a lower cost, and enforcement of tax rebate discounting will be beefed up. Canadians will therefore be able to make freer, more informed choices. The price of discounting will fall, which will help lower income Canadians who are the main clientele of discounters.
Free enterprise and consumer interest both depend on the provision of choice. The steps which the Government is proposing will ensure that better choices are available in the Canadian market-place, in that Canadians will have the information they need to take advantage of those choices.
The practice of tax rebate discounting will continue because it can still provide a service for which there exists a market demand among Canadians. At the same time, this total package of measures will correct serious shortcomings, the impact from which has been felt by those least able to bear it. It will protect both legitimate business interests and the consumer's right to fairness and choice. I am confident that it will receive swift passage by the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to replace my colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic (Mrs. Killens), the Official Opposition critic for Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I rise today to speak about this bill because, as you will know, Mr. Speaker, our colleague is now convalescing. I am certain that the Hon. Member for Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic would have liked to have been here to take part in this debate and we all regret her
December 5, 1985

absence from this House. 1 believe that all the Hon. Members here today will join me in wishing her a very quick recovery and a return to this House early in the new year.
I would like to apply myself, as my colleague would certainly have done herself, to making the most constructive possible criticism of the proposals and amendments regarding income tax discounting.
The speech made by the Minister today is well balanced, and I think that if he is a victim of circumstances, it is because he wants to please everybody at once, which is certainly very difficult to do in politics.
However, Mr. Speaker, you will understand that I am happy to take part in this debate since it concerns a Department which I have had the privilege and the honour to head in the past.
There is no need to remind this House that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was created by the previous Liberal Government, and today's debate confirms in my opinion the necessity and the appropriateness of having such a Department.
When the Minister announced his proposals regarding income tax discounting, many comments were made by various organizations. I believe that one of the most important of these comments, and I would like to repeat it in this House, is that the Minister apparently did not have the courage to go as far as he could have gone, and I would like to explain what I mean by that. Each year, Canadians must report their income, and several taxpayers are in a position to claim an income tax refund because they paid in too much. And if they paid in too much, it is because in many cases their income is so small the Government cannot ask them to contribute any more without jeopardizing their own survival.
We in the Liberal Party would like people who have paid too much income tax to get back this overpayment in full. Nobody in my view should be penalized or exposed to any income loss because of a slow-moving Government machine, in this case the Income Tax Refund Department of Revenue Canada which unfortunately may take not just weeks, but months to deliver. At the present time, such is the situation as we must admit, and the working paper published by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in June 1985 provides evidence of that. Mr. Speaker, the decisions announced by the Minister on November 21 do not address the problem from that angle. Instead, it accepts what I would call an improved status quo allowing or giving an opportunity to the most in need to go on using a service that is charging rates that are, if not criminal, at least too high for low-income people.
You will understand, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberal Party feels the time is ripe for a specific policy that would allow those who are entitled to an income tax refund to receive the full amount, or at least as large a part as possible without having to wait far too long. And if that were impossible, there has to be at least a guarantee that the most in need are offered
Tax Rebate Discounting Act
one of the most competitive rates, rather than what could be called loan shark rates.
What I think is needed is an overall vision, an overall understanding of the problem and its solutions. It is my hope that this House, and especially the Government will wish to relinquish that piecemeal approach put forward by the Minister, and take alternatives that may require more courage indeed but that will prove more fair and just for all the taxpayers involved.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to dwell too long on the history of that problem faced by this House. But as far as the assignment of income tax refunds is concerned, the situation now is different from the one we had in 1978, when the Act went into force.
In the early seventies, the practice of tax rebate discounting was not regulated or even recognized by law or by a professional association. So it was not unusual for people seeking instant tax refunds to be charged 40, 50, 60, or even 65 per cent of the rebate expected. Calculated over the long term, these rates were entirely out of proportion to the amounts being discounted. Tax rebate discounting was criticized because of its usurious rates and what I would qualify as flyby-night operations. It was therefore not surprising that a number of organizations defending the interests of low-income groups made representations to the provincial authorities, who then, for various reasons, made their own representations to the Federal Government, asking it to take steps to deal with the abuse occurring in these operations.
That was the situation we had in 1978. The phenomenon was not very widespread but demanded immediate attention. The Tax Rebate Discounting Act was a way to regulate these activities by putting a 15 per cent limit on the rates that could be charged for early income tax refunds. In fact, the cost of filing the income tax return was included in the 15 per cent, and everyone expected this practice to cease and disappear altogether, since the profit margin had obviously become too narrow for anyone to get a reasonable return. That was unfortunately not the case. On the contrary, the legislation gave an aura of legitimacy to the practice of tax rebate discounting and more and more people were using this service. When the child tax credit came on the scene, it made the business expand even more and became a kind of bonanza for all those establishments involved in the discounting trade. Mr. Speaker, at the time, the Tax Rebate Discounting Act was adopted unanimously. In fact, it took only 25 minutes for the House to adopt all three stages of the Bill.
This time, I don't think a decision should be made without careful consideration. We want legislation that considers all aspects of the problem and the potential consequences in relation to the various options available. I think this can be
9222

December 5, 1985
Tax Rebate Discounting Act
achieved by sending the Bill to a legislative committee, far removed from partisan considerations. 1 believe the Minister is acting in good faith, and I think the Minister has a problem that he wants to solve in a fair and equitable manner. And I hope the proposals we will make within the framework of a legislative committee will be given due consideration and, if possible, accepted by the Minister. We hope that witnesses will appear before the committee when it examines this legislation in detail.
In 1981, need I remind the House, the legislation was amended so that the 15 per cent charged to cover the transaction not be considered as criminal. Calculated on a yearly basis, this rate could reach over 60 per cent, which is now considered an illegal rate in Canada. At the time, all this appeared quite acceptable because there were still relatively few customers. I must say that because of the economic crisis which we lived through in the early 1980s, the increased number of unemployed, the high rate of inflation and the reduction in the purchasing power of most Canadians, many people decided to avail themselves of tax rebate discounting services to make quick transactions or to meet, in a number of cases, their most basic needs. It should be recognized, therefore, that the cession of the right to an income tax reimbursement has now become an instrument which makes it possible for a number of taxpayers in need of cash to find some at this time of the year, and I think that this time of the year is a good sales season because of the cut prices offered consumers by both manufacturers and retailers. We must therefore recognize that these services have become greatly popular. But this should not prevent us from considering the economic predicament of the people who avail themselves of these services. In fact, two-thirds of the customers of the tax rebate discount industry earn $8,000 or less a year.
In 1985, we have experienced the fourth consecutive year in which the number of Canadians living below the poverty line has increased. There are now approximately 4.35 million Canadians living below the poverty line. Included in this important group are women who are heads of single parent families.
1 am very sensitive to the fact that poverty has become a woman phenomenon in Canada. And if the Hon. Member for Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic (Mrs. Killens) was here to deal with this Bill, I am sure that she would pay special attention to this phenomenon and explain it far better than I. And I feel that we, as Parliamentarians, and especially the Minister, on behalf of the Government, should deal with these 33.5 per cent of poor families headed by women, and that we should not overlook this context when we deal with the income tax rebate discounting problem.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, I am referring to poverty, because it is the most disadvantaged who generally use these services. As a matter of fact, the percentage of male clients who declared an annual income of less than $8,000 was 61.6 in
1983. More disquieting still, the percentage of female clients who declared an annual income of less than $8,000 was 82 in 1983.
In fact, the average income of all clients is $5,573, whereas the average income of all female clients is $1,625. It tells us a lot, Mr. Speaker! It is obvious that the underprivileged are the main users of the services of that growing industry. More specifically, female heads of single-parent families constitute the majority of those users.
Can we still say that the measures introduced by the Minister improve the ot of discounters's clients? One thing we can say for sure is that these measures will attract even more clients. It is my opinion, but not mine alone, for discounters themselves think so. Most Members will agree that it is impossible to save money with incomes like that. Most people with such low incomes live in dire misery. Can we really talk about protecting the consumer's choice, as the Minister tells us in such cases? We in the Liberal Party do not believe there is really a choice to be made. That is why the rates the discounters ask for their services must be, in our opinion, as low as possible when they are figured out on an annual basis.
What makes the matter even worse, in my judgment, is the growth of the industry.
In 1979 there were 7,000 discounting transactions because, as compared with today's figures, in 1985, there have now been 515,000 transactions.
I suggest that such a phenomenal growth can only endure, given the Minister's propositions. All the more so since he said he intends to advertise and tell the public about this service. Well, I hope Canadian taxpayers will not have to foot the advertising bill.
I hope the Minister will make agreements with the industry-doing very well as it is, thank you-so that it will pay for the advertising campaign. In my estimation, those firms should pay for the information we must give the public in that field.
It is important to realize that if we cannot or do not want to abolish this service, we have to make sure that the rates stay as low as possible.
I see no reason to believe the Minister received any overwhelming support from the Provinces, or for that reason from the various interest groups on those proposals.
The various interest groups' response to the working paper was not as spontaneous and unanimous as stated by the Minister. Quite the opposite, many spokesmen for the low-income class felt that the solution was wrong, because they would have preferred a total ban on discounting, in conjunction with a faster income tax refund procedure.
Provinces also were not unanimous, because Quebec as we know does not allow that kind of operation. Any amount owed citizens by the Government is deemed unassignable in Quebec. And at this moment, two other Provinces have some doubts,
December 5, 1985

because they are considering measures more stringent than those announced by the Minister, and I understand they are even considering outright banning of such practices.

We should remember that in the United States, such a practice does not exist. I would like to cite the following American legislation:
Any person who is an income tax preparer who endorses or otherwise negotiates (directly or through an agent any check made in respect of the taxes imposed by subtitle A which is issued to a taxpayer other than the income tax return preparer) shall pay a penalty of $500 with respect to each such check.
[ Translation]
I think that the United States, which we could call the cradle of free enterprise, are giving us a very good example in that respect. Indeed, the Americans would not allow that kind of operation, recognizing that overpayments to the state belong exclusively to the overpaying citizens. They do not accept that such funds be diverted, and there is a fine for violators that discourages any discounting operation. In my view, such an example should motivate the Minister in this debate.
Finally, I would like to outline the proposals we could put forward, in the Official Opposition, and it is indeed my wish to be somewhat more specific as to our position on that issue of the assignment of rights to income tax refunds.
Concerning the announcement made by the Minister that the child income tax credit would be paid in a number of instalments, this is not enough in my view. The idea certainly is interesting, except that the income tax child credit is still discountable. Low-income groups and Provinces would hope for a ban on any discounting transaction of that credit. It is also the opinion of the Liberal Party, Mr. Speaker, and the prohibition must also apply to the child tax credit, otherwise, we have reason to believe that there may be further abuses in the future.
Moreover, in my opinion, the rates are still too high for most customers of this service. If you want to borrow $1,000 or even $2,000, you will discover that not many Canadian banking institutions are willing to lend you the money. The efforts made by the Minister show that he is aware of these difficulties. However, we are going to find out that interest rates on these loans are relatively high since they apply over a one year period.
This is why, after the bill has been referred to a committee, we intend to move an amendment to provide for a maximum set rate.
The Minister has used all his accounting expertise to try and keep the amounts as low as possible, but I think that when he is dealing with amounts of over $300, if there is no set maximum rate, some people may lose too large a part of the money which is theirs and which should come back to them, if not in its entirety, at least as completely as possible.
Tax Rebate Discounting Act
The problem of discounting, and I shall close with this in a short while, hides another problem, that of providing access to financial institutions for small wage-earners. 1 do not necessarily want provisions in this regard to be included in this legislation, but I simply want to point this out and to make sure that the Minister will accept to consider this issue in the near future.
Our Party will want to look closely at the cost of the proposed measures to the Canadian taxpayer, as compared to the cost of strict cancellation. I believe this would be most interesting and useful for the Members of the legislative committee.
I think the Minister will want, also, to continue having a yearly study of the tax rebate discounting industry in order to get an idea of the impact of the proposed measures and to find out the social and economic characteristics of consumers. This could be done with a view to taking action should the problem get larger and more serious, instead of getting better.
If the child tax credit is excluded entirely from any discounting transaction, I believe that we should continue paying it in one or at the most two payments, rather than in a series of installments, because studies have shown that the money is used to buy more expensive goods like furniture or appliances, to pay dentist's bills or to get essential clothing for the smaller children in the family.
To sum up, I think I should repeat to the House that it is very important to us that we exclude the child tax credit from any tax rebate discounting. I hope the Minister will be willing to try and convince his cabinet collegues of the necessity of it. If he fails to do so, the Bill he is defending today will not have the results he is seeking. I think that when the original Act was passed unanimously at the end of the 1970's, we were all convinced that it would resolve the problem of the neediest in our society. We soon realized that such was not the case.
I dare hope that the Bill introduced by the Minister will not result in a proliferation of tax rebate discounting activities in Canada. I hope that this Bill will make it possible, as suggested by the Minister, for Canadian taxpayers to get their refunds more quickly and also provide a better protection for all those who unfortunately cannot wait for their income tax reimbursement, want to get their cash as soon as possible and who, therefore, rely on companies which provide them with a service at a cost, which, in my opinion, is much too high. It is with this in mind that I conclude my remarks. I wish to assure the Minister of the constructive co-operation of the Official Opposition, provided he accepts a number of amendments which we feel are absolutely essential.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to begin my comments in respect to this Bill by protesting the timing of its presentation. We now know how poorly Parliament acted in 1978 when it passed the legislation which this Bill proposes to replace. In 1978 the Bill was passed in just 20

December 5, 1985
Tax Rebate Discounting Act
minutes by the House. The entire policy-making process in the Civil Service and the working out of the details took just one month. We are now repeating the same process because the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) has delayed so long bringing this Bill forward.
I asked the Minister questions about this a year ago and brought to his attention the dimensions of the problem. I told him of the thousands of people who are adversely affected by the law. I was told then that the Minister was keeping a close watch on the procedures and that he would be doing something fairly quickly. We were then told there would be a discussion paper in June. Of course, the discussion paper did not appear at that time.
We were finally promised that we would see a Bill in September. We did not receive the Bill until the end of November and we are debating it today for the first time. We are debating it with a gun to our heads because we are told it must receive second reading today. We are told that if the Bill does not reach committee and if it is not dealt with there and brought back before Parliament adjourns for Christmas, in January when the tax returns go out people who have used discounters in the past, and who will probably want to use them again, they will be able to go to the discounters who will be able to charge them the fees at the old rates which were so reprehensible. Thus, we have to agree to get this Bill through today, although we are not satisfied with it.
We do not think the Bill deals with the problem as it should, and neither do different organizations in the country. 1 refer to the consumers' associations, the church organizations, national anti-poverty organizations-the Minister is shaking his finger. We have talked to these organizations and we know what they have said. What they have said is that they want this Bill through, not because they think it meets all the problems but because the provisions of this Bill are better than the old one. It is not because they are satisfied with it.
I ask the Minister why we had to wait until the end of November to deal with the problem? After all, the problem was brought to the attention of the former Government. If I have the time, I may have something to say about the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and what he said on this subject when he was the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.

It was written February 8, 1983 and concerned the Tax Rebate Discounting Act. The then Minister replied on March 7, 1983. I would like to read one paragraph from his letter. He said, and I quote:
While the 15 per cent rate may not satisfy all interested parties, it allows legitimate lenders to carry on business, and accordingly allows Canadian consumers to decide whether or not to use a service which is now controlled by legislation.
That is what the Minister said then.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: That sounds like a good answer.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
And that is exactly the kind of answer which we are getting from the present Minister who says he wants the free enterprise system to work, that he wants people to have a choice. But telling people that they have a choice in this kind of situation reminds me of a saying by that famous French author, Anatole France. He said: "The laws of France permit every French person, rich and poor, to exercise the option to sleep under a bridge, if they want". This Bill gives people an option but the Minister knows very well that the only people who are likely to exercise that option to go a tax discounter are not the wealthy people, not the middle income earners, nor even the working people who have full-time permanent jobs. The people who go to the tax discounter-and the numbers have been doubling and tripling every year so that we are now talking about close to a half a million people-are the poor people, the people who are living on welfare, the single mothers who have children. They have living on the edge of poverty. They are living in a crisis situation. When it comes towards the fourth week of the month they have run through their welfare cheques. They are the people who go to the tax discounters and they are the people who are going to continue to go to the tax discounters and will continue to be ripped off by these tax discounters.
We are talking about a very large amount of money. It is pretty obvious that these hundreds of thousands of Canadians who go to tax discounters have been paying, as we have all said, extremely high interest rates for loans. Because that is what they are; they are loans from the tax discounter and those companies are getting rich.
Two of the richest companies H & R Block, and Ben-Tax, which is a subsidiary of Beneficial Finance, together handled more than 80 per cent of discounting transactions in 1983. These two companies have increased their volume of business over the past four years and their profits have soared dramatically. H & R Block recently reported its profits for the year ending April 30, 1985. These reports make interesting reading and I hope the Minister will pay some attention to them. Its revenues were over $59 million, up from $37 million the year before. Revenues from tax discounting were $25.2 million, up from $18.2 million. Profits were $5.9 million, up from $4.9 million. So there was a 38.5 per cent increase in revenue from tax discounting operations in one year.
December 5, 1985

That is what we are dealing with. We are dealing with the problems and difficulties of close to half a million of the poorest Canadians who are being ripped off by corporations. I cannot blame the corporations. They are operating under the provisions of the laws which we enacted in 1978 and they will operate next year under the provisions of the laws we are going to pass this month. However, they are making tremendous profits from the backs of the very poor.
We ought not to kid ourselves that these are anything but loans, and I say forced loans given to the very poor by these tax discounters. The Department has always known this. When the previous Bill was being debated in 1978, a representative of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said: "This type of transaction is a disquise loan. It may have a term of two months or an indeterminate term, but it is nonetheless a loan transaction". What we are proposing today is to make some changes in the amount of payment which will cause the interest rate to drop somewhat.
Revenue Canada has, by its efficiency, shortened the period that people have to wait to, in many cases, four weeks or a little less. If we take into account the fact that it no longer takes eight or more weeks to deliver these cheques, the real interest rate is very high.
Under the old provisions a formula was included for the calculation of the interest rate in Schedule 1. It is this simple interest rate which has led to a good deal of confusion because it was always presumed that tax returns would take four months to be processed. In the debate which took place in committee in 1978, a Government witness said that the assumption in the Act is that there is a term of four months. That is the outside limit of what it would take for a return to come back. So on every form which was printed, in accordance with Schedule 1 of the Act, a box had to be filled in for the customer showing the discount at an annual rate, and giving the standard annual interest rate for the calculation. So the tax discounter was able to reprint it in his form, and we have a sample from Ben-Tax showing the real interest rate to be 62.8 per cent. That is a lot of money to pay for a loan to a clerk making the minimum wage.
This 62.8 per cent, as large as it is, not an accurate rate of interest for those transactions, because in the vast majority of cases it did not take nearly that long to deliver the cheque. Today Revenue Canada processes returns not within four months but within an average of four weeks. We have been informed that Revenue Canada processed the first 31 batches of 1984 returns in an average of just 4.3 weeks. This is particularly relevant to our discussion because the T-l specials under which most child tax credits are claimed, have been processed in 3.7 weeks and the T-l general form has been processed in an average of 4.7 weeks.
So we can see that the old interest rates in the Act, as it was, were dangerously misleading, and though the 62.8 per cent interest which those companies charged exceeded the minimum interest rate under the Criminal Code, it required a special provision in the Act to exempt this rate of interest in tax discounting transactions.
Tax Rebate Discounting Act
What are the true rates of interest we are talking about? We went to the research branch of the Library of Parliament and asked them to prepare some calculations for us. We appreciate the help they gave us. They said that under the old interest provisions, which this Bill will change, the annual interest rate was 62.8 per cent for a four-month term, 91.6 per cent for a three-month term, 165 per cent for a two-month term, and 600 per cent if it were processed in one month. Mr. Speaker, discounting at 15 per cent really means loans at interest rates of between 62 and 600 per cent. Under his new proposal the Minister is still permitting the 15 per cent charge on the first $300. Under the so-called reform which the Minister is bringing forward the new rates are blended rates because, as I have indicated, the amount charged is 15 per cent on the first $300 and 5 per cent on the balance.
Again we asked the Library of Parliament to analyse the new rates for some typical amounts. They said that for a $100 rebate processed in four weeks the interest rate would actually be 727 per cent and so on. These rates are grotesque rip-offs of the people who can least afford it but have no other choice if they need the money immediately. It is a revelation to some of us that so many poor people need money immediately, especially to some Members who have not paid attention to the problems of their constituents.
The Government does not seem to worry about that. Two-thirds of the people who used discounters in 1984 had incomes of less than $8,000. They are the working poor and the people on welfare. Waiting for money is a hardship for most of them and the supposed choice of using or not using the discounter is really no choice at all for many of them because they live so close to the poverty line.
When the Conservatives were in Opposition they were critical of the system we had. The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was very indignant about the role being played by tax discounters. He was quoted in The Citizen on February 23, 1983, as saying that it is a shame and a tragedy that taxpayers have to give up $150 of their $1,000 tax refunds. Is he not ashamed of the fact that today, under the proposal made by the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the same taxpayer with a $300 refund will lose the same 15 percent which he lost three years ago? Is it not a shame that the improvement of Revenue Canada in processing tax forms really means that tax discounters will be lending at even higher rates than previously because they will get their repayment that much faster?
A committee of this House expressed itself very clearly on tax discounting. In its report on child and elderly benefits dated April 2, 1985 the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs said:
The federal Government, in consultation with the provincial Governments, should take steps to outlaw tax rebate discounters.
That is a committee on which the substantial majority of members were and are Conservatives. They got the same information that was available to the Minister and they recog-

December 5, 1985
Tax Rebate Discounting Act
nized the tremendous injustice in the system and called for the outlawing of the tax rebate system.
The Government has made much of being the champion of taxpayers in the country with its taxpayers' bill of rights. When I look at what the Minister is proposing in this Bill I have to assume that when the Conservative Government was talking about the taxpayers' bill of rights it was talking about a bill of rights for taxpayers in the middle and upper income brackets. We do not find any mention of taxpayers who use income tax discounters in this document, but surely these taxpayers should be protected too. Presumably this Act is supposed to protect their rights, but does it do that? Let us test that assumption.
A person using a tax discounter is entitled to a professional evaluation of his income tax in return for paying his fee for service. Of course, this does not happen. Any person in Canada can operate as an income tax discounter and have no standards to meet beyond the ability to lend money. A person using a tax discounter should not have to pay interest rates higher than the Canadian law allows. This does not happen either since the Act with which we are dealing today specifically excludes the Criminal Code provisions forbidding interest rates higher than 60 per cent.
A person should have an alternative to using a tax discounter. This, of course, is what the Conservatives promised with its slogan of "free choice". However, Mr. Speaker, the Minister has not delivered that. There are no provisions in this Bill or any other that would make an income tax return collateral for a loan at commercial rates. The Minister has talked prior to today and again today of getting credit unions and caisse populaires interested in these kinds of loans, but we have yet to see any firm commitments and programs which will make an alternative to tax discounters possible on a large scale. Surely the Minister and his Department had the time to meet with the credit unions, the caisse populaires and the banks to work out, if possible, a system whereby people who needed to get their money quickly could do so and at a legitimate rate.
We can also ask whether people who use tax discounters get the same kind of consideration which the declaration of taxpayers' rights says they are entitled to from Revenue Canada. Are they entitled to full information, impartiality, courtesy, consideration, and the presumption of honesty, all of which the declaration states? We know they have not had that up until now. Although the Minister said in his speech today that he was going to try to provide some of these factors, they certainly do not exist at the present time.
That is not the reality of tax discounting which is really far closer to the atmosphere of a pawn shop than an office at Revenue Canada. The truth is that tax discounters have a minimal law to satisfy in terms of service. As I have indicated, by using the figures of H & R Block, they do extremely well by doing as little as possible. This legislation does not ask much of them.
We believe that this Bill does not deal with the problem. We say that knowing that we have the support of many organizations which have expressed their views. We know that the
consumers' association is not satisfied with this Bill. We know that the National Anti-Poverty Organization is not satisfied with the Bill. We know, Mr. Speaker, that the provincial Ministers of Consumer Affairs cannot be satisfied with this Bill because they were unanimous in their belief that at least the discounting of child tax credits should be prohibited. The Minister did not listen to them.
This Bill does not meet the needs of the Canadian people who have been hurt so much by the process of tax discounting. It was bad in 1978 and became a tremendous tragedy with the implementation of the child tax credit. It was that provision which led to the tremendous increase in the number of people who go to tax discounters. The ones who are hurt the most are those people who must use tax discounters because the only income tax refund they get is from the child tax credit. They still will not be dealt with fairly as a result of this legislation.
This debate concerns what really happens to the child tax credit as an effective social payment and how it is delivered to Canadian mothers, particularly low-income mothers. The child tax credit in its present form of a refundable tax credit on federal income tax has been in place since 1979. It is not accident that the increasing value of the child tax credit has coincided with the growth of income tax discounting.
The refundable credit was valued at $218 in 1979 and will be worth $384 in 1985. It will be enriched further until 1988 to offset losses of family allowances indexing and will then be capped at $524 in 1988.
Clearly that credit is an important social program and has been equally important to income tax discounters since it has fueled the growth of tax discounting. For example, 43 per cent of all those who used a tax discounter in 1983 claimed a child tax credit and 83.5 per cent of women who used discounters claimed the child tax credit.
There is a clear link to low incomes for child tax credit claimants who used discounters. In 1983, 21 per cent of women claiming the credit had family incomes below $2,000. Imagine a family with an income of less than $2,000 having part of their tax credit discounted. Not only is it a disgrace that we permit that tax credit to be discounted, it is a disgrace that they have such a low income. As well, 24 per cent of women claiming the credit had family incomes below $2,000 and no spousal income. Women who have income like this have no attraction to discounters beyond the child tax credit and other credits.
Obviously, we are talking about the very poor, people who desperately need money. They will likely be ready to file a return in January before Revenue Canada is prepared to handle the return unless this Bill, with all its deficiencies, is passed within the next couple of weeks.
There is no freedom of choice for these people. No bank will give them credit for a loan. There is no way that they can use their income tax return as security except by going to the tax discounter. The only choice these people have is between one discount and another, and all their rates are extortionate.
December 5, 1985

We now have some idea of who is getting hurt by tax discounters when we see that in 1983, 45,000 women with no spousal income and personal incomes below $2,000 used tax discounters. We also know from the same records from the Ministry of Consumer and Corporation Affairs that of the $41 million earned by tax discounters, between $15 million and $20 million came from child tax credits. That is almost half. It is quite clear that this program is haemorrhaging in its waste of public money.
This Bill does nothing to rectify the situation. Despite the Minister's statements about freedom of choice, it does not give a woman with little income beyond child tax credit a low-interest alternative. There is no way that she can use her tax return as loan security. There is no ban on tax discounters taking child tax credits although this was a proposal agreed to by Ministers of Consumer Affairs in Manitoba last September. There is even a delay on the new payment scheme for child tax credits which will not go into effect until 1987. These tax discounters do not only rip off the child tax credit, because many provincial Governments have provincial income tax credits designed to help those who are less well off. In British Columbia there is the renter's tax credit. In Alberta there is a renter's tax credit. In Ontario, there is a property tax credit, a retail sales tax credit and a pensioner's tax credit which was later replaced by a grant. In Manitoba there is a property tax credit and a cost of living tax credit.
According to the Canadian Tax Foundation's book, Canadian Tax Policy, it has been demonstrated that these tax credits inject fairness into the tax system in these provinces by providing: "The greatest relief for lower income tax payers and the least relief for high income tax payers". The Canadian Tax Foundation study makes no mention of what happens when tax credits from the provinces are discounted and 15 per cent of these benefits are still taken away on the first $300 from those who qualify.
It is not surprising that the Minister of Consumer Affairs in Manitoba, Mr. Rowland Penner, was quoted in the Winnipeg Free Press in February of this year as saying:
These are supposed to be benefits to help the really poor. If they are losing as much as 15 per cent of this support program then we are failing recipients to that extent.
This legislation is failing the poor. We now have the means to rectify this failure but it is not accomplished by this Bill. The Government's defence of the integrity of tax credits is to allow a charge of 15 per cent on the first $300 and 5 per cent on the rest of the refund. It is still failing the poor.
By this lack of consideration for provincial jurisdiction in income tax matters, the federal Government is telling the provinces that they must abandon tax credits if they wish to see the integrity of their programs protected. It also means that the approaches toward a negative income tax system for helping the poor is hopelessly vulnerable to tax discounters.
This is how the authors of Canadian Tax Policy summed up the impact of Canada's tax system on the working poor:
There is virtually no federal program designed to assist the working poor. They do receive preferential treatment under the personal income tax system and
Tax Rebate Discounting Act
may be tax exempt owing to various deductions and exemptions. But they do not receive income transfers. Some provinces (for example, Ontario) provide a modest amount of tax credits to low-income persons, ostensibly to offset provincial sales and property taxes.
Rather than those people benefiting as the provinces have proposed, they are ripped off because the Government will permit tax discount operations to continue.
It is quite obvious that what little the tax system is prepared to transfer to the working poor will still be subject to the activities of the discounter. Is that how the Conservatives wish to treat the vast numbers of people who keep small and marginal businesses operating in Canada? Those poor people who will be ripped off will have less money to purchase goods from small businesses.
Bill C-83 comes no closer to helping the working poor. In fact, tax discounting will make the situation far worse for the working poor.
Canadians cannot afford this legislation. The poor cannot afford to be short changed as they will be under the provisions of this Bill. subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CANADA PENSION PLAN ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CANADA PENSION PLAN ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to amend the Canada Pension Plan Act to
1.	provide more flexibility so that all contributions can be taken into consideration at the discretion of the Minister; and
2.	extend the time in which an individual can apply for a disability pension to 12 months or such longer period as approved by the Minister.
She said: Mr. Speaker, Canada's provincial Treasurers will be meeting with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in Edmonton soon and an important item on the agenda will be amendments to the Canada Pension Plan. The Canada Pension Plan was introduced in the mid 1960s and improvements or amendments to it have always been slow and difficult to realize. This is so, in part, because of the requirement that all amendments be not only approved by Parliament but also by two-thirds of the provinces with two-thirds of the population of Canada.
Another difficulty in bringing about improvements to the Canada Pension Plan has been the financial reason. Over the years provinces have borrowed very extensively from the Canada Pension Plan. I believe the cumulative amount which Ontario has borrowed over the years is now at about $14.5 billion. Under those circumstances, the provinces tend to resist any further costs.
The Canada Pension Plan provides workers and their families with a basic level of earnings related protection agains the contingencies of retirement, disability and death. The Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform which reported at the end of 1983 raised the question of whether disability benefits belong in a pension plan, but did not make a recommendation on whether disability provisions should continue to be found within the Canada Pension Plan or should be in a separate program. However, the committee did recommend an increase in the amounts and it that respect 1 quote from the report:
-current benefit levels do not reflect relevant living standards. As MPs we believe that a significant and early increase in disability benefits is essential.
The question of disability benefits was also discussed by a special committee which considered matters relating to the disabled and the handicapped during 1983. That committee had some very far-reaching recommendations which I hope we will see in law fairly soon. One of them was that a comprehensive disability insurance program be established and integrated
Canada Pension Plan Act
with the Canada Pension Plan and Quebec Pension Plan. Another was a proposal to change the definition of disability so that it would exclude fewer people. Another was to allow earnings on a sliding scale while a person is in receipt of benefits. These are all very progressive recommendations but what we are left with now is very much more restrictive.
Disability benefits under the Canada Pension Plan consist of a flat rate portion and an earnings related portion of 75 per cent of the imputed retirement pension. Disability benefits are payable in the case of severe and prolonged disability as a result of which the person is incapable regularly of pursuing any substantially gainful occupation. Clearly, that is a very restrictive definition.
First, the words "incapable of pursuing substantially gainful occupation" imply, really, giving up hope. The injured person is unwilling to face the fact that he or she may be unable to pursue any gainful occupation. Relatives are willing to encourage that kind of expectation. Doctors are reluctant to take away hope from people. So what tends to happen after the disability is that the patient tries every conceivable chance of rehabilitation and further treatment. He tries to go back to work and then a year has passed and he or she is no longer eligible for benefits because the application must be made within 12 months of becoming disabled. That is in the statute and there is no ministerial discretion. That is the first matter which I would like to see changed. I would like to see greater flexibility in the time for applying for disability benefits.
The second matter concerns the requirement that the contributions to the Canada Pension Plan must have been made in a fixed timeframe. The timeframe varies but essentially, for most people, they must have contributed within five of the last 10 years. Women, particularly, often fail to qualify, if we take on the year they have been ill and then, perhaps, four years when they may have been home with young children. Time and again they have failed to qualify even though they may very well have had 10 years of contributions. The contributions should be looked at in another timeframe.
Having dealt with a number of people who have lost their eligibility to Canada Pension disability benefits, either because of the 12 month limit or because of the timeframe in which they should have contributed, I am proposing that the Government include in its next meetings with the provinces for discussion proposals to bring some flexibility into these two matters in particular.
These are two very specific issues, and while my motion only concerns those two issues, 1 am not, of course, suggesting that that is the end of the debate on the needs of the disabled. 1 would in fact like to see a much more comprehensive plan in place, as was advocated by the all-Party committee on the disabled. However, I think the proposals I am putting forward are simple and practical and it might be possible to get agreement on those with the provincial Ministers concerned.

December 5, 1985
Canada Pension Plan Act

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CANADA PENSION PLAN ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) which would essentially, if it were to be adopted by both the federal and provincial Governments provide more flexibility so that all contributions could be taken into consideration at the discretion of the Minister and, second, extend the time at which an individual could apply for a disability pension to 12 months or such longer period as might be approved by the Minister.
As the Hon. Member for Trinity has already pointed out, the Canada Pension Plan has a very stringent definition of disability. It can only be applied to persons who can never again be re-employed. We also know from a whole variety of reports which are available to Governments, both provincial and federal, that among those individuals who have been unfortunate enough to leave the workforce because of a disability and have applied to the Canada Pension Plan for a benefit under that plan there is widespread poverty. Those persons are poor for a number of reasons. First, because they applied for a disability pension under the CPP they are not permitted to accept any form of work while they are in receipt of the benefit and, second, of course-and this has been argued very strongly in the Obstacles report, to which the Hon. Member for Trinity referred-is that simply because you become disabled does not mean that your expenses come down, by any means. In fact, more often than not when one is disabled one incurs additional expenses which an able-bodie person would not normally have.
I was a member of that special committee, along with other Members from all sides of the House, and in our report we said that within the insurance companies, disability is called "the living death" because the family of the disabled person is deprived of a regular income as if the person were dead but is left with equal or greater expenses because the person is still living. That may be a harsh way to put it but I think it is the reality of many people once they become disabled on the job.
There is also no doubt that trying to reform Canada's pension plan is an extremely slow process. I recall that when I came here in 1980 there was the National Pensions Conference. I was fortunate enough to be a delegate from the House to that conference. To say there was no consensus arrived at at that conference would not be to exaggerate. But something which did come through from the conference was the need to reform Canada's pension system. Since then we have had the second national conference on pensions, and we still have not arrived at any form of consensus.
In fact, I just quickly ran through some notes I had on pension reform and found that the then Minister of National Health and Welfare, Monique Begin, announced proposals on December 7, 1981 while she was at the United Nations. She set out a whole series of proposals to improve the disability benefits under the Canada Pension Plan.
The following day there were news reports emanating from the Treasurer of Ontario at that time, Mr. Frank Miller, who very bluntly and strongly said that he did not think that disability benefits should properly fall under the Canada Pension Plan but should come from somewhere else. He did not define where the "somewhere else" would be. I just say that to illustrate the difficulty there is in getting provincial-federal agreement on improvements to the Canada Pension Plan, and that is required as we all know under that plan.
In spite of the special committee on the disabled, and announcements from Ministers of National Health and Welfare over the years, including the present Minister, not too much has been accomplished. I believe that is why I and other Hon. Members welcome the proposal made by the Hon. Member for Trinity which will again give us the opportunity to speak about some of the problems associated with that issue in the House and, hopefully, bring some pressure to bear on the Parties who are responsible for the negotiation to go at it in a much more serious way.
We all have constituents who have had great difficulty with the Canada Pension Plan. When they have attempted to apply for a disability pension they found out fairly quickly that the interpretation of the section of the Canada Pension Plan means that they have to be practically comitose in order to receive a benefit. If they are fortunate enough to receive a benefit, the benefit itself is totally inadequate to allow a person to live with any degree of dignity or financial independence.
The proposals in the Obstacles report received broad support from provincial Governments, the federal Government and all kinds of Canadians. Yet, those proposals have not yet been adopted.
In February of 1983 the advisory committee on the Canada Pension Plan, which reports to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), presented the Minister with further proposals on how to improve disability benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. In that report it was pointed out that there was widespread poverty among persons in receipt of that benefit.
They made two suggestions to improve that. I will use the figures that they used in 1982, although they are out of date now. They said that disability benefits under the Canada Pension Plan could be improved by increasing the flat rate component from its present level of $70.68 per month to a much higher level such as the equivalent of the Old Age Security pension of $227.73 per month which prevailed from January to March of 1982.
The second recommendation was that raising the earnings-related component from 75 per cent of the contributor's imputed retirement pension to 100 per cent-that would be from $230.74 a month to $376 per month-would make the benefits to these individuals equal to a benefit that they could receive at age 65. It would, in effect, double the pension income for disabled individuals.
This is something that is sorely needed. This has been recognized by many groups and individuals who have been requested by the Government to conduct examinations into the Canada Pension Plan and, indeed, the entire pension system. I think the House would be doing a service to Canada's present
December 5, 1985

disabled, as well as future disabled Canadians, if we were to agree today to refer the motion of the Hon. Member for Trinity to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. In that way we could once again ensure that the problems faced by that group of Canadians are receiving the kind of public attention they fully deserve.
I do not think I need say too much more. I think the Member who introduced the motion put the case very well. I only wanted to indicate my support for that measure.
