speakeroldname: Mrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CANADA PENSION PLAN ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can only applaud the motion by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Ms. Nicholson) regarding the advisability of expanding eligibility for disability benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. However, I think this measure alone would not solve all the problems connected with disability coverage, and I would prefer to seek a solution based on a comprehensive review of our disability benefit system.
Before examining the system and its shortcomings, I would like to give a brief overview of the situation facing many disabled individuals. First of all, it is extremely difficult to establish an accurate profile of the disabled in Canada. It is difficult because we have no single definition of what disability is. Even programs for the disabled are based on widely varying definitions of disability. Furthermore, our statistics on the disabled population in Canada are very limited. However, the few data we do have point to a situation that is extremely disturbing. It is estimated that about 12.5 per cent of Canadians are disabled to some extent. Eighteen per cent of disabled individuals between the ages of 15 and 64 have a serious disability. It is also true that both the percentage and the seriousness of the disability increase with age. For instance, it is estimated that only 5 per cent of the disabled are under 15, while about 30 per cent are over 65.
Economically speaking, the disabled are certainly one of the least advantaged groups of our society. There are a number of factors that account at least partially for this situation. We see that the unemployment rate among disabled individuals who are able to work tends to be higher than among the general population. It is also true that individuals who are unable to work usually have a very low income. According to a 1981 survey of recipients of disability benefits under the Canada Pension Plan, their average income from all sources was equal to or below the low-income threshold established by Statistics Canada.
The precarious financial situation in which the disabled find themselves is not due to a lack of Government programs for this particular group. The disability benefits system in Canada includes a range of programs that provide workers with income protection in case of disability. However, the most effective programs have been designed to meet specific objectives such
Canada Pension Plan Act
as protecting workers in case of accidents on the job or meeting our obligations to disabled veterans.
I would now like to give a brief description of the main programs that constitute our existing disability benefits system. These programs can be classified in two major categories: general disability programs and category programs.
The general disability programs are those under which benefits are payable regardless of the cause of disability. It is the case, for instance, of the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan. Those are mandatory social insurance programs under which wage earners and the self-employed have guaranteed coverage in case of disability. Eligibility for disability benefits however is strictly limited because of the limited scope of the definition of that word as used in those plans.
There are also voluntary private insurance programs for prolonged disability. These programs cover about 43 per cent of the work force. Generally speaking, they provide a substitute income roughly equivalent to 60 to 75 per cent of the income earned before disability. It should be noted however that such programs provide for an integration formula under which benefits are reduced when the recipient gets other disability benefits.
Social assistance is the last program in the category of general programs. Social assistance benefits are paid to the needy, no matter what the cause may be. These programs are administered by the provinces, but the federal Government shares the costs.
As to the second group of programs offering income protection in case of disability, it also includes so-called category programs. These programs pay benefits to people in particular circumstances. An example would be the system of provincial workers' compensation programs. They compensate workers who suffer from disability due to a work accident. Category programs also include disability pensions paid to veterans, car accident insurance plans, and compensation for victims of criminal acts.
This description of the Canadian system of disability benefits would indicate that ours is a relatively complete and efficient system. I am sorry that I have to say that such is not the case, unfortunately. Our system has major short-comings which can be grouped around three major problems. The first of these problems stems from the difficult task of determining what a disability is. The universal income related programs such as the Canada Pension Plan, the Quebec Pension Plan or the long term disability insurance plan essentially provide benefits in case of a very serious disability, but do not provide any benefit to people suffering from a partial disability.
Specific programs providing compensation for work-related or automobile accidents provide benefits in case of total or partial disability. However, these benefits are paid only if the disability is the result of a specific cause, like a wound suffered or an illness incurred on the job, or in an automobile accident.

December 5, 1985
Canada Pension Plan Act
In fact, it is not always possible to identify the single cause of disability. For instance, certain types of cancer can be the result of smoking and or working conditions. When in doubt as to the cause, unfortunately, the application for benefits may be turned down. Naturally, this all or nothing approach is a source of much criticism.
The second problem concerns the target population. People who are not earners can hardly expect protection except for provincial social assistance, legal aid, or private insurance programs. The problem concerning self-employed workers is different. As I said, nearly all wage earners are covered by the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan. They can also receive benefits as compensation for a work-related accident or under a private insurance plan. The fact that these people are seeking similar objectives inevitably result in an over-lapping protection. Such a situation generally arises when an invalid person is eligible for benefits under more than one program. Some of the results of this over-lapping of measures are an increase in administrative costs for the system and a more complicated procedure for the applicant.
The third and last major short-coming of our system, but not the least, concerns the limit of benefits paid. It should be emphasized first that the level of these benefits vary widely from one program to another. The programs which cover the greatest number of people are unfortunately those which also pay the lowest benefits. In fact, the social assistance program which has the widest coverage provides only a minimum income to the needy. Social assistance benefits are subject to a means test and do not take into account the salaries previously paid to the worker.
As for the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans, they provide a level of income based on previous earnings. The maximum amount of the disability benefit in these cases represents approximately 20 per cent of the average industrial wage. In addition, the great majority of recipients have benefits much lower than the maximum amount of benefits payable. About 14 per cent of disability benefit recipients must depend on provincial welfare programs to meet their needs. This clearly indicates that the level of disability benefits under the CPP is quite inadequate.
On top of this problem, there is the difference in the disability benefit rates of the two plans. I am certain that this question will be debated during the federal-provincial discussions on pension reform. Moreover, neither plan offers complementary programs to meet special needs.
Workmen's compensation programs also replace, but more substantially, the previous earning income of the disabled. However, the maximum level of benefits is limited by the ceiling of insurable earnings which varies with the provinces.
However, these programs offer the most comprehensive range of services to meet the special needs of the disabled.
Private insurance programs for extended disability also provide a very high rate of replacement of previous earnings. However, there is little protection against inflation in the long term. On the other hand, these programs pay benefits related to special needs under certain circumstances.
I trust that improvements can be made to the existing system. Indeed, this is why the federal and provincial governments are actively working on a comprehensive review of disability benefits. Under its terms of reference, the task force must identify the weaknesses of the present system and define possible options to provide a complete disability insurance system. The task force is expected to report to the federal and provincial social services ministers by the end of this year.

speakeroldname: Mr. Girve Fretz (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Mines)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CANADA PENSION PLAN ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to respond to the motion today presented by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson). The Government recognizes that Canada's disabled population needs improved assistance. We are already taking steps to facilitate this goal.
In this regard I would like to draw the attention of Hon. Members to changes to the disability tax deduction which were announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his Budget address of May 23, 1985.
Effective for the 1986 and subsequent taxation years, this special income tax deduction will be available to any individual who is certified by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) as being a person who, during the year, was suffering from a severe and prolonged mental or physical impairment. This is a major improvement in that currently only the blind and those who are confined to a bed or wheelchair are eligible for the special disability deduction.
As the Minister of Finance pointed out, if the effect of the disability is to markedly restrict the person in activities of daily living, and if the disability has lasted or can be expected to last for a continuous period of at least 12 months, the person will be eligible for the tax deduction. About 185,000 people are expected to benefit under this broader definition, a substantial increase over the 65,000 current claimants.
There is no doubt that one of the major problems facing the disabled today is inadequate income support. The above change is evidence of both our recognition of this serious problem and our commitment to find a solution. Nevertheless, the Government knows that despite the fact that a myriad of programs exist to assist disabled persons, this group remains among the poorest people in Canada.
I think it is obvious that the motion before us today is an attempt to alleviate this situation. The Hon. Member has identified the Canada Pension Plan disability provisions as being in need of improvement. Her criticism is not with the level of benefit or the definition of disability which are the two areas most commonly looked at with regard to CPP disability benefits. Instead, I think the Member has asked the Govern-
December 5, 1985

ment to modify the eligibility criterion that requires a disabled CPP contributor to meet the minimum contributory requirements and to extend the date at which disability can be deemed to have occurred. These are two changes which, even though they may seem of minor significance at first glance, could improve the financial situation of at least some disabled persons.
Before commenting in detail on the two proposals contained in this motion, 1 believe it would be useful to first review the current legislative requirements for the receipt of a CPP disability pension. As well, I want to outline for Hon. Members why legislators at the time the plan was introduced in the mid-1960s chose the criteria they did.
In order to qualify for a disability benefit, the CPP currently requires a contributor to have contributed for a minimum of five calendar years and the lesser of: 5 of the last 10 years and, in total, at least one-third of the number of years in the individual's contributory period; or 5 of the last 10 years and, in total, at last 10 years.
The underlying rationale for these minimum contributory requirements was twofold. First, it was felt that because of the substantial flat-rate benefit which makes up a portion of the CPP disability pension, it was only reasonable to require that contributors demonstrate a substantial attachment to the paid labour force.
Second, given that the CPP is designed to provide contributors and their families with a measure of protection against the loss of earnings income, it was felt that a test of recent attachment to the labour force was not unreasonable. However, since the introduction of the CPP in 1966 the minimum contributory requirements have been criticized and proposals have been made for changes.
I am sure that it will not surprise Hon. Members to hear that the Hon. Stanley Knowles, who is well known to all of us for his concern and efforts on behalf of disadvantaged Canadians, made one such proposal as far back as 1977. During a 1977 meeting of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, Mr. Knowles suggested possibly reducing the minimum contributory requirement for receipt of a CPP disability pension to one year. At that time the then Minister of National Health and Welfare agreed to refer the subject to the Canada Pension Plan advisory committee.
In a June 1980 report to the Minister, the advisory committee rejected in principle the proposal by which a single year's contribution to the CPP would entitle a contributor to coverage at any future date, regardless of the contributor's future labour force participation. The committee felt that some test of recent labour force attachment was still required. Instead, what the committee recommended was that the current rules be maintained and supplemented by an additional rule which would allow a contributor to qualify for disability coverage if he or she had made one valid contribution, either in the year of disability or in the immediately preceding year. This proposal was formally submitted to the provinces for consideration.
Canada Pension Plan Act
In this regard, I should point out that a major change to the CPP requires the approval of both the federal Government and two-thirds of the provinces having two-thirds of the Canadian population.
However, a decision on this and other CPP disability benefit improvements was deferred until such time as a federal-provincial study could be completed on the feasibility of introducing a comprehensive disability protection scheme.
As Hon. Members may remember, such a scheme was recommended by the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped in its 1981 report, Obstacles. I believe that report has been alluded to in the Chamber today. I am pleased to note that the study is expected to be submitted to federal and provincial Ministers of social services by the end of this year. This study, along with proposals to improve CPP disability benefits, will be included in upcoming federal-provincial consultations on comprehensive pension reforms.
In addition, it may interest Hon. Members to know that the minimum contributory requirements for receipt of a disability pension under the Quebec Pension Plan were amended effective January 1, 1984, for persons between the ages of 60 and 64. Persons in that age group, who are no longer able to do the job they had prior to disability, are entitled to receive a QPP disability pension if they have contributed to the plan for a minimum of seven years. However, while the recent labour force attachment test has been abolished under the Quebec Pension Plan, it must be kept in mind that it is only for a small group of QPP contributors, the near elderly.
Let us now turn to the Hon. Member's suggestion that there be an extension in the time limit allowed for the determination of when an individual can be deemed to be disabled. Currently, a CPP contributor cannot be deemed to be disabled earlier than 12 months before the month of application for a disability pension.
At the time the CPP was introduced, legislators recognized that in many cases disabled persons would not apply for CPP disability benefits as soon as they became disabled. There could be many reasons for such a delay, not the least of which is the fact that it takes time to recognize and accept that one meets the severe and prolonged definition of disability under CPP. Thus, it was felt only reasonable to allow some measure of retroactive determination. However, while some retroactivity was desirable, it was recognized that it would be very difficult in many cases to determine exactly when a contributor became disabled for CPP purposes. A maximum of 12 months prior to the month of application was deemed to be a reasonable length of time to allow for a retroactive determination of disability. As Hon. Members can appreciate, it would be difficult to administer a provision which had no fixed date.
The Hon. Member's motion suggests that the time period be left up to the Minister's discretion, but 1 am sure that we can all recognize the potential inconsistency of protection that such an approach could create. Nevertheless, it may be that a longer period of time should be allowed, such as 24 or perhaps even 36 months, and that this issue could be included in the federal-provincial consultations on CPP changes.

December 5, 1985
Canada Pension Plan Act
There may be another reason disabled workers are not applying for CPP benefits as soon as they might. I think we should ask ourselves whether Canadians are delaying application for CPP disability benefits through ignorance. Is it that they are unaware of the protection afforded by the CPP? If so, this is the problem that must be dealt with. Canadian workers and their employers pay for the CPP. They pay so that when they meet one of the contingencies for which a CPP benefit is available they can receive the needed earnings replacement the CPP provides. New and innovative efforts are being made by the Department of National Health and Welfare to acquaint CPP contributors of their rights under the plan. Those who are entitled to CPP benefits should apply for and receive these benefits at the first opportunity, and every effort is being made to ensure that individuals know this.
The Hon. Member is to be complimented today for her concern for Canada's disabled. I assure her and all Canadians that the Government shares this concern. Every effort will be made to bring about much-needed improvements for disabled persons in the very near future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak today on the broader issues associated with the motion to amend the Canada Pension Plan put forward by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson).
In response to the concerns raised in Obstacles, the report of the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped, federal and provincial Ministers of social services agreed in February, 1982 that prior to proposing any legislative initiatives, they would establish a joint federal-provincial task force on income protection.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the study was to identify means to provide adequate benefits to all disabled and handicapped Canadians, both in and out of the work force.
The first phase of this study was completed as mandated with the task force submitting its report to Ministers in September 1983. I understand that the Ministers have agreed to continue the work of the task force. It is expected that the second phase of this study will be completed in time to meet the December 1985 completion date.
In closing, I want to emphasize that this Government is prepared to make specific changes. I compliment my colleagues from Trinity on her excellent motion.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: TRANSPORT A) REQUEST THAT EUROPEAN TRAVEL VOUCHERS BETABLED BY MINISTER B) DEMAND THAT TRAVEL DOCUMENTS BE PRODUCED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to spend the few minutes allotted to me to deal with the trips made last summer by the Hon. Minister for Environment, the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mrs. Blais-Grenier).
Several documents were obtained recently under the Freedom of Information Act, which clearly show that although the main purposes of the trip made by the Hon. Minister, despite the fact that such purposes and such meetings had been cancelled to the Minister's knowledge, she nevertheless decided to travel "through the Europes". As it seems in this matter, the more documents that get out, the clearer it becomes that originally there was a reasonable purpose, an official purpose for the Minister to go to Europe. We can appreciate that the Minister added to that official activity other ones of a personal and touristic nature, which she probably intended to carry on at her own expense. It appears however, that when the main reason for the trip was cancelled, the Minister was in quite a dilemma, namely: should she then forgo the interesting, entertaining, touristic part of the trip? And this is where, unable to resist the temptation, she decided to proceed nonetheless with her European tour.
I have here a few documents that are interesting to quote. For instance, I have in hand a telex from our embassy in Stockholm to External Affairs here in Ottawa, dated March 27, which was before the April trip, and I am simply quoting from the telex:

There is a 98 per cent chance that the Stockholm ministerial meeting will be postponed. Please advise if we are correct in presuming that if the ministerial meeting is postponed. Minister Blais-Grenier's visit to Sweden will also be postponed.

The embassy was them assuming that were the official part cancelled, the Minister would forgo her trip. But we know that the opposite happened. Indeed, the Minister went in spite of that.
I have here another telex to External Affairs from the Canadian embassy in Moscow: it may sound a bit strange but I should like to quote a few words from it. It is stated that certain Soviet officials whose names I will not mention since they are not needed for the purposes of the discussion, "cannot therefore greet Mrs. Blais-Grenier in Leningrad, although the
December 5, 1985

Soviet party appreciates the touristic character of the visit to Leningrad". Those are documents written by federal officials.
I have another one here sent to Helsinki from External Affairs, in which one instruction is given:

-would like to emphasize the private nature of the trip.
And at that point, the Minister having requested that the host country look after hotel reservations:

We are advised that Moscow will not process item like this. Please contact Intourist in Helsinki for arrangements.

So even host countries did not want to get involved.
I could go on with that kind of quotes. But I feel that what we now need to know is, what did the Minister pay for herself, because we have several invoices which we examined and it does not appear that during the entire trip, except for one part that is quite identifiable where the Minister visited Corsica at her own expense, it seems. And there, I believe it because no invoices were tabled or obtained under the Freedom of Information Act to indicate that the Canadian taxpayers paid for anything with respect to that trip. So that part of the journey, where she went to Corsica, is not involved.
But, on the other hand, for all the other parts of the two trips we know of, the one in April and the one in June, we have hotel vouchers showing continuity. We have limousine vouchers, and there is no evidence whatsoever as to how the Minister herself would have paid part of the costs. So we are wondering what part the Minister should pay back to the Canadian taxpayers.
Finally, I would simply stress that coming from a Minister in a Government that is preaching austerity, restraint, it is bad example to go sightseeing at the taxpayers' expense. In my view, on the one hand the Minister should reflect on what she did, and on the other the head of the Government should put out stringent guidelines to make sure such things do not happen again.

AGRICULTURE-FARM DEBT-GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) FARM GROUPS' DEMAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 25, I put a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) as follows:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. A week ago Saturday, 800 farmers demonstrated in front of the Minister's constituency office in St. Thomas to protest the lack of action on the farm debt crisis. Can the Minister say when the Government is going to take action as demanded by the seven responsible farm groups, on a comprehensive farm debt moratorium and farm credit arrangements legislation?
I did not get much of a response from the Minister that day, and I will refer to that later.
Essentially, many of the people who were at that demonstration were tobacco farmers from that area as well as beef farmers from the Bruce Peninsula and the Bruce-Grey riding. They were all protesting the lack of action on the part of the Government on farm credit legislation and on the extension of the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation loans to other loans. Of course, we received no answer from the Minister.
The demonstrators who are in front of the Parliament Buildings today are mainly tobacco growers. It is little wonder that they are demonstrating. They have seen a litany of broken promises. For instance, back in June, 1984, they met with the then Hon. Member for Haldimand-Norfolk (Mr. Bradley) and the then Minister of Agriculture. At that time the Minister gave a commitment that there would be national marketing and legislation for tobacco.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) wrote a letter to a Mr. Garry Balthes in November of 1984 which reads:
Dear Garry:
Thank you for your letter of August 14.
I was pleased to have an opportunity to meet with you and your co-workers from the concerned farmers group during the campaign, and can assure you that our government will be acting quickly to establish a National Tobacco Marketing Agency, as well as other measures designed to assist tobacco producers.

December 5, 1985
Adjournment Debate
A rally took place on November 9 at which about 800 farmers protested and demanded action. One of the farmers with whom I communicated is in his seventies. He said that it was the angriest and most ugly farm demonstration he had seen since the 1930s.
Last weekend, on November 30, there was another rally in Delhi. 1 asked the Hon. Member for Haldimand-Norfolk why he did not attend that rally. I did this because farmers were contacting me to complain about the fact he was not attending. Of course, he brought in the explanation that he had to go to a Santa Claus parade in an adjoining community.
Next Tuesday, December 10, there will be an even larger rally here in Ottawa to protest the lack of action with respect to the establishment of a farm marketing agency and all of the other things which farm groups are waiting on. They are waiting because of a litany of broken promises and broken commitments by the Government.
When we raise the subject in the House the Minister just gives a smart alec answer such as he did on November 25. On that day he said he did not take any action because the House was not sitting that week. That type of answer may receive great guffaws and a great response from back-benchers on the government side, but it certainly does not give the Minister credibility. Nor does it put him in a favourable light with farmers who are facing the most devastating financial crunch since the 1930s.
What we see from the Government and the Minister is a litany of broken promises and broken commitments. We have not seen any action with respect to establishing any of the agencies about which the Government has talked. The farmers are getting bloody mad. They will continue to rally. They will continue to demand that the Government take action. They were promised this years ago. Then the Conservatives came to power and the action is simply not forthcoming. It is just stall, stall, stall. When action does come about it is in the form of a dribble and really amounts to no action at all.
1 am acting on behalf of these people tonight demanding that the Government move ahead with these demands and keep the commitments it made, not only in the election campaign but several times since. There has been no action forthcoming up to this point in time.
